title: Create foundation
content:
1. Create the Foundation Stack in the AWS Console If this is the first time ECS is used in your lab account, open AWS CloudShell and check whether the ECS service-linked role exists:
aws iam get-role --role-name AWSServiceRoleForECS --query 'Role.Arn' --output text If the command returns NoSuchEntity, run the command below to create the role. If it returns AccessDenied, ask your AWS administrator to check and create the role using an identity with iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole permission for ecs.amazonaws.com.
aws iam create-service-linked-role --aws-service-name ecs.amazonaws.com After creating it, wait for IAM to propagate before continuing. If you already encountered Unable to assume the service linked role and the tina-staging stack is in ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, confirm it is the lab stack you just created, delete the failed stack, wait for DELETE_COMPLETE, and then recreate it. Stacks in CREATE_FAILED may offer a Retry button in the Console. See Service-linked roles for Amazon ECS in the AWS documentation .
If you want CloudFormation to create the role in an account that does not yet have AWSServiceRoleForECS, add the snippet below to the existing Resources: section of foundation.yml. Place ECSServiceLinkedRole at the same level as Cluster, then add DependsOn to the Cluster resource. Keep all existing Properties of Cluster unchanged. When creating the stack, acknowledge IAM resource creation if the Console prompts you.
ECSServiceLinkedRole: Type: AWS::IAM::ServiceLinkedRole DeletionPolicy: Retain Properties: AWSServiceName: ecs.amazonaws.com Cluster: Type: AWS::ECS::Cluster DependsOn: ECSServiceLinkedRole # Keep the existing Cluster Properties right below. This role is shared across the account. If the role already exists or you recreate the stack after deleting it, use the original template together with the CloudShell check above. Retain keeps the role when the stack is deleted, so declaring it again may fail with a duplicate-name error. See the CloudFormation ServiceLinkedRole documentation .
Go to CloudFormation → Stacks → Create stack.
Open foundation.yml on GitHub , choose Download raw file, and save it as foundation.yml. In CloudFormation, select Upload a template file → Choose file, pick the downloaded file, and click Next.
In the poor-frog/TINA repo, this file lives on the feat/s3-ephemeral-workspaces branch at deploy/aws/foundation.yml. The link above points directly to commit 7d6bba8… so you can download just this file for the Console step.
CloudFormation screen selecting foundation.yml to create the VPC and foundation. Enter Stack name = tina-staging and click Next. This exact name is required for the workshop because it determines the prefix of the three ECR repositories and several policies in the application templates. Leave all other options at their defaults and click Next → Submit. Wait for CREATE_COMPLETE; if an error occurs, open the Events tab, locate the first CREATE_FAILED entry, and inspect the reason. Open the Outputs tab and note VpcId, PublicSubnetIds, AppSubnetIds, DataSubnetIds, AppRouteTableIds, ClusterName, and StagingRecordingsBucket. The workshop uses this bucket for recordings and temporary invocation files. CloudFormation Outputs of the foundation stack: VPC, subnets, cluster, and bucket; mask the account ID if shown. 2. Verify Created Resources Go to VPC → Your VPCs and locate the VPC matching VpcId from the stack Outputs. Go to Subnets and filter by that VPC. You should see two public subnets, two app subnets, and two data subnets across two Availability Zones. Six subnets created by the foundation stack, showing VPC and Availability Zones. In ECS → Clusters, confirm that the cluster from the Outputs exists. The stack’s S3 bucket has Block Public Access enabled, encryption turned on, and a lifecycle rule that expires files under runtime-invocations/ after one day. Do not manually edit resources managed by the stack.

title: Overview and acceptance
content:
What Will You Build? In a fresh AWS account, CloudFormation creates a two-Availability-Zone VPC, an ARM64 ECS Fargate cluster, private S3 buckets, NAT Gateway/VPC Endpoints, RDS PostgreSQL, Valkey, CloudFront + WAF, an internal ALB, and all ECS services (Terminal, Gateway, Meeting/Admin API, Runtime, Bot, VieGem ASR, Agent/MCP/Flows, and optional LiveKit/VieNeu Voice). You can copy the prebuilt linux/arm64 images from GHCR (workshop-arm64) straight into your own ECR via CloudShell (see 5.4A ) or build them from source. Names include staging because some templates and ECR permissions require that prefix; all resources still belong to your own account.
Browser → CloudFront/WAF → Internal ALB → Terminal (ECS Fargate) ↓ Gateway + meeting/admin API ↓ ↓ ↓ Runtime/ECS bot RDS Valkey ↓ ↓ ↓ S3 VieGem Agent/MCP/Flows To evaluate the lab, verify that the stacks created in your own account succeed, the services reach their desired state, and the sign-in/meeting flow works. A stack in CREATE_COMPLETE only confirms that AWS provisioned the resources—it does not prove that all TINA functionality works.
After completing the sections below, this screenshot shows the stack list in your lab account:
TINA stacks you created and their statuses in CloudFormation. The next screenshot shows the service status inside your cluster:
ECS services in your lab account, including desired and running tasks. Acceptance Criteria Your CloudFront URL loads the TINA site and allows signing in with a test Google account. The ECS core, runtime, and terminal services run stably, and the terminal target group is healthy. Create an authorized test meeting and observe the bot; if ASR is enabled, verify the transcript and note any errors encountered. Understand the cost drivers and cleanly delete all resources when finished.

title: S3, ECR and ARM64 image build
content:
1. Verify your S3 bucket In S3 → General purpose buckets, find the StagingRecordingsBucket name from the tina-staging stack outputs. This bucket was created privately in your account; keep Block all public access enabled. Under Management → Lifecycle rules, verify the expiration rule for the runtime-invocations/ prefix. Do not upload private data for screenshots.
Recordings bucket in your lab account, showing Block Public Access enabled and the lifecycle rule. 2. Create the remaining ECR repositories The foundation stack already created tina-staging/bot, tina-staging/runtime, and tina-staging/meeting-api. In CloudShell, create the four additional required repositories:
for name in terminal gateway admin-api viegem; do aws ecr create-repository --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --repository-name "tina-staging/$name" \ --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE --encryption-configuration encryptionType=AES256 done If a repository already exists in your account, verify its name and permissions, remove it from the loop, and run the command for the remaining ones. Do not change the tina-staging prefix: several execution roles in this pinned template version grant read access specifically to this prefix.
Fast option (recommended — skip Sections 3, 4, and 5, avoid EC2 OOM / SSM Offline): Instead of launching an EC2 builder to compile Docker images (which requires heavy RAM), run the block below directly in CloudShell to copy the prebuilt linux/arm64 images from GHCR into your ECR under tag $TINA_TAG (ws-v1), then jump straight to 5.4.2 :
export AWS_REGION="${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}" export TINA_ACCOUNT="${TINA_ACCOUNT:-$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)}" export TINA_TAG="${TINA_TAG:-ws-v1}" if [ ! -x /tmp/crane ]; then curl -sSL "https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/releases/latest/download/go-containerregistry_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz" | tar -xz -C /tmp crane fi ECR_REG="${TINA_ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com" aws ecr get-login-password --region "$AWS_REGION" | /tmp/crane auth login "$ECR_REG" -u AWS --password-stdin for name in terminal gateway meeting-api admin-api runtime bot viegem; do /tmp/crane copy "ghcr.io/poor-frog/tina-${name}:workshop-arm64" "${ECR_REG}/tina-staging/${name}:${TINA_TAG}" done 3. Create an IAM instance profile for the builder (only if building on EC2) The following commands create a temporary EC2 role with the Systems Manager policy and ECR push permissions scoped to tina-staging/* repositories. Run this once in CloudShell using an identity with IAM management permissions:
cat > "$HOME/tina-workshop/builder-trust.json" <<'EOF' {"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]} EOF cat > "$HOME/tina-workshop/builder-ecr.json" <<EOF {"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[ {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"ecr:GetAuthorizationToken","Resource":"*"}, {"Effect":"Allow","Action":["ecr:DescribeRepositories","ecr:DescribeImages","ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability","ecr:InitiateLayerUpload","ecr:UploadLayerPart","ecr:CompleteLayerUpload","ecr:PutImage","ecr:BatchGetImage","ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer"],"Resource":"arn:aws:ecr:${AWS_REGION}:${TINA_ACCOUNT}:repository/tina-staging/*"} ]} EOF aws iam create-role --role-name tina-workshop-builder-role --assume-role-policy-document "file://$HOME/tina-workshop/builder-trust.json" aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name tina-workshop-builder-role --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore aws iam put-role-policy --role-name tina-workshop-builder-role --policy-name TinaEcrPush --policy-document "file://$HOME/tina-workshop/builder-ecr.json" aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name tina-workshop-builder-profile aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile --instance-profile-name tina-workshop-builder-profile --role-name tina-workshop-builder-role If a role or profile with the same name already exists, stop and verify ownership before using it; do not overwrite a role belonging to another system. After creating them, wait for IAM propagation before selecting the profile in EC2.
4. Launch an ARM64 build instance in the EC2 Console Go to EC2 → Instances → Launch instances. Name it tina-workshop-builder. Choose Amazon Linux 2023, architecture 64-bit (Arm); for example, t4g.small (Free Plan compatible; larger instances such as m7g.2xlarge require a Paid Plan or higher quota). Smaller RAM instances require the 8 GiB swap file in Section 5—or use the Fast option (crane copy in CloudShell) in Section 2 to avoid running out of memory while building bot/viegem. This instance incurs charges while running. Key pair: choose Proceed without a key pair. Under Network settings, select the tina-staging stack VPC, one public subnet from PublicSubnetIds, and enable Auto-assign public IP. Create a security group with no inbound rules, keeping outbound rules for Internet access. Configure storage: for example, 200 GiB gp3; click the Advanced button in the top-right corner of the Configure storage panel to enable encryption (Encrypted → Yes). Under Advanced details → IAM instance profile, select tina-workshop-builder-profile; enable IMDSv2 required if shown. Click Launch instance. Wait until the instance state is Running and Systems Manager detects it. Select the instance → Connect → Session Manager → Connect. If the tab cannot connect, verify the IAM profile, SSM Agent, public IP, route to the Internet Gateway, and outbound HTTPS access. 5. Build and push images from EC2 Run the commands in this section inside the EC2 Session Manager session, not in CloudShell. Add an 8 GiB swap file first to prevent out-of-memory hangs (which cause SSM Agent to go Offline while building bot/viegem), install Docker and Git, then switch to a root shell for this temporary build session:
sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile && sudo chmod 600 /swapfile && sudo mkswap /swapfile && sudo swapon /swapfile sudo dnf install -y docker git sudo systemctl enable --now docker sudo -i cd /root git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/poor-frog/TINA.git tina-source cd tina-source git fetch origin feat/s3-ephemeral-workspaces git checkout --detach 7d6bba8109f6eac51c0d8241a7083e3e364cf59d git rev-parse HEAD docker buildx version Download the workshop build script: download tina-ecr-build.sh , or click the ▶ Click to expand… line below to reveal and paste the block directly into EC2 to create /root/tina-ecr-build.sh without downloading an external file:
Fast deployment tip: If you prefer not to build Docker images on EC2, see 5.4A Quick Deploy with 1 CloudFormation Stack to copy the prebuilt set of 15 linux/arm64 images (including VieGem and Voice) directly from GHCR into ECR right from CloudShell.
▶ Click to expand & copy the complete /root/tina-ecr-build.sh script cat > /root/tina-ecr-build.sh <<'EOF' #!/usr/bin/env bash # SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 set -Eeuo pipefail readonly EXPECTED_REVISION=7d6bba8109f6eac51c0d8241a7083e3e364cf59d SOURCE_DIR="$PWD" REGION="${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}" readonly PREFIX=tina-staging TAG="${TINA_IMAGE_TAG:-ws-$(date -u +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)}" PLAN_ONLY=0; WITH_VIEGEM=0; WITH_ADDONS=0; WITH_FULL=0 while (($#)); do case "$1" in --source) SOURCE_DIR="$2"; shift 2 ;; --region) REGION="$2"; shift 2 ;; --with-viegem) WITH_VIEGEM=1; shift ;; --with-addons) WITH_ADDONS=1; shift ;; --full) WITH_FULL=1; WITH_ADDONS=1; WITH_VIEGEM=1; shift ;; --plan) PLAN_ONLY=1; shift ;; *) echo "Unknown option: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac done SOURCE_DIR="$(cd -- "$SOURCE_DIR" && pwd -P)" REVISION="$(git -C "$SOURCE_DIR" rev-parse HEAD)" [[ "$REVISION" == "$EXPECTED_REVISION" ]] || { echo "Wrong source revision: expected $EXPECTED_REVISION, found $REVISION." >&2; exit 1; } images=(terminal gateway meeting-api admin-api runtime bot) ((WITH_ADDONS)) && images+=(agent-api agent-reach agent-worker mcp flows) ((WITH_VIEGEM)) && images+=(viegem) printf 'Revision: %s\nRegion: %s\nECR prefix: %s\nTag: %s\n' "$REVISION" "$REGION" "$PREFIX" "$TAG" ((PLAN_ONLY)) && { echo 'Plan only: no image was built or pushed.'; exit 0; } ACCOUNT="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --region "$REGION" --query Account --output text --no-cli-pager)" REGISTRY="${ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${REGION}.amazonaws.com" WORK_DIR="$(mktemp -d)" trap 'rm -rf -- "$WORK_DIR"' EXIT mkdir -p "$WORK_DIR/source" git -C "$SOURCE_DIR" archive --format=tar "$REVISION" | tar --exclude='.env' --exclude='.env.*' --exclude='.env.keys' -xf - -C "$WORK_DIR/source" SRC="$WORK_DIR/source" aws ecr get-login-password --region "$REGION" | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY" >/dev/null push_image() { local name="$1" dockerfile="$2" context="$3"; shift 3 local image="$REGISTRY/$PREFIX/$name:$TAG" docker build --platform linux/arm64 --file "$SRC/$dockerfile" --tag "$image" "$@" "$SRC/$context" docker push "$image" } if ((WITH_FULL)); then push_image terminal clients/terminal/Dockerfile . --build-arg NEXT_PUBLIC_TERMINAL_MODE=workspace-pilot else push_image terminal clients/terminal/Dockerfile . --build-arg NEXT_PUBLIC_TERMINAL_MODE=meetings fi push_image gateway core/gateway/services/gateway/Dockerfile . push_image meeting-api core/meetings/services/meeting-api/Dockerfile . push_image admin-api core/identity/services/admin-api/Dockerfile core/identity/services/admin-api if ((WITH_FULL)); then docker build --platform linux/arm64 --file "$SRC/core/runtime/Dockerfile" --tag tina-workshop/runtime-base "$SRC/core/runtime" push_image runtime deploy/aws/workspace-pilot.Dockerfile . --target runtime --build-arg RUNTIME_BASE=tina-workshop/runtime-base --build-arg AGENT_BASE=tina-workshop/runtime-base --build-arg WORKER_BASE=tina-workshop/runtime-base else push_image runtime core/runtime/Dockerfile core/runtime fi docker build --platform linux/arm64 --file "$SRC/core/meetings/modules/join/Dockerfile.env" --tag tina/meet-join-env:dev "$SRC/core/meetings/modules/join" push_image bot core/meetings/services/bot/Dockerfile . --build-arg "TINA_IMAGE_VERSION=$REVISION" if ((WITH_ADDONS)); then if ((WITH_FULL)); then docker build --platform linux/arm64 --file "$SRC/core/agent/services/agent-api/Dockerfile" --tag tina/v012-agent-api:staging-voice "$SRC" docker build --platform linux/arm64 --file "$SRC/deploy/aws/voice-worker.Dockerfile" --tag tina-workshop/agent-voice "$SRC" push_image agent-api deploy/aws/workspace-pilot.Dockerfile . --target agent --build-arg AGENT_BASE=tina-workshop/agent-voice --build-arg RUNTIME_BASE=tina-workshop/agent-voice --build-arg WORKER_BASE=tina-workshop/agent-voice else push_image agent-api core/agent/services/agent-api/Dockerfile . fi push_image agent-reach deploy/agent-reach/Dockerfile deploy/agent-reach if ((WITH_FULL)); then docker build --platform linux/arm64 --file "$SRC/core/agent/worker/Dockerfile" --tag tina-workshop/worker-base "$SRC" push_image agent-worker deploy/aws/workspace-pilot.Dockerfile . --target worker --build-arg WORKER_BASE=tina-workshop/worker-base --build-arg RUNTIME_BASE=tina-workshop/worker-base --build-arg AGENT_BASE=tina-workshop/worker-base else push_image agent-worker core/agent/worker/Dockerfile . fi push_image mcp core/meetings/services/mcp/Dockerfile core/meetings/services/mcp push_image flows core/flows/Dockerfile . fi if ((WITH_VIEGEM)); then ASSETS="${TINA_VIEGEM_CACHE:-$HOME/.cache/tina-workshop/viegem-fsmn}" mkdir -p "$ASSETS" docker build --platform linux/arm64 --build-arg TORCH_VARIANT=cpu --file "$SRC/deploy/transcription/viegem/Dockerfile" --tag tina/v012-viegem:staging-cpu-base "$SRC" docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 --mount "type=bind,src=$ASSETS,dst=/assets" tina/v012-viegem:staging-cpu-base python install-models.py --directory /assets push_image viegem deploy/aws/viegem.Dockerfile deploy/aws --build-context "viegem_assets=$ASSETS" fi for name in "${images[@]}"; do digest="$(aws ecr describe-images --region "$REGION" --repository-name "$PREFIX/$name" --image-ids "imageTag=$TAG" --query 'imageDetails[0].imageDigest' --output text --no-cli-pager)" printf '%-14s %s/%s/%s@%s\n' "$name" "$REGISTRY" "$PREFIX" "$name" "$digest" done EOF chmod +x /root/tina-ecr-build.sh Once /root/tina-ecr-build.sh is in place, run a dry-run build plan (--plan):
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 export TINA_IMAGE_TAG=ws-v1 bash /root/tina-ecr-build.sh --source /root/tina-source --region "$AWS_REGION" --plan Verify the source revision, Region, repository prefix, and tag. The --plan flag does not build or push anything. To test transcription with VieGem under non-commercial license terms, also build the model image with --with-viegem. The VieGem model is licensed under CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 and the Gemma terms; review the model card and license notes before using it. If those terms do not fit your use case, omit --with-viegem, skip the VieGem stack, and leave the transcription parameters empty in the core stack.
bash /root/tina-ecr-build.sh --source /root/tina-source --region "$AWS_REGION" --with-viegem The build downloads dependencies and model files from the Internet, which can take significant time and disk space. With the option above, the script builds 6 application images plus 1 VieGem image, pushes them to ECR in the account attached to the instance role, and prints their digests. The source is archived from the pinned commit; the script never copies local .env files. If the command fails, check the first error; when retrying after a partial push, set export TINA_IMAGE_TAG=ws-v2 because tags are immutable, and update TINA_TAG accordingly in CloudShell.
In ECR → Private repositories, open tina-staging/terminal or tina-staging/bot and verify the tag and digest:
Your ECR repository showing the image tag and digest after the build. After confirming that all required images are present, terminate the EC2 builder if you no longer need it; ECR retains the pushed images. Do not delete volumes or resources belonging to other instances.

title: WAF, CloudFront and ALB
content:
1. Create a Web ACL in the AWS Console Go to AWS WAF & Shield → Web ACLs → Create web ACL. Name it tina-workshop-acl. For Resource type, select CloudFront distributions; Web ACLs of this type are managed in us-east-1. Leave the associated resources list empty because CloudFormation will attach the distribution later. Under rules, you can add the AWS Managed Rules Core rule set for practice and keep the default action set to Allow. WAF rules and requests may incur charges; tune and test rules before production use. Keep the default metrics settings and click Create web ACL. Open the newly created Web ACL and copy its ARN. Do not use the ARN of a Regional Web ACL. CloudFront-scope Web ACL created, with the account ID redacted in the ARN. CloudFront-scope Web ACL details, with the account ID redacted in the ARN. 2. Deploy CloudFront and the internal ALB In CloudShell, replace the placeholder value with your Web ACL ARN:
WAF_ARN='PASTE_YOUR_CLOUDFRONT_WEB_ACL_ARN' VPC_ID="$(stackout tina-staging VpcId)" APP_SUBNETS="$(stackout tina-staging AppSubnetIds)" PREFIX_ID="$(aws ec2 describe-managed-prefix-lists --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --filters Name=prefix-list-name,Values=com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing \ --query 'PrefixLists[0].PrefixListId' --output text)" printf 'Prefix list: %s\n' "$PREFIX_ID" If the prefix list prints None or is empty, check your Region before proceeding. Deploy the stack:
aws cloudformation deploy --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name tina-ws-edge --template-file "$TINA_SRC/deploy/aws/staging-edge.yml" \ --parameter-overrides "VpcId=$VPC_ID" "AppSubnetIds=$APP_SUBNETS" \ "CloudFrontOriginPrefixListId=$PREFIX_ID" "WebAclArn=$WAF_ARN" Wait for CREATE_COMPLETE, which can take a few minutes because of the CloudFront VPC origin. Open the StageUrl from the stack outputs with /edge-health appended: you should see TINA_EDGE_READY. Visiting the root path at this point may return 503 because Terminal has not been deployed yet.
stackout tina-ws-edge StageUrl In CloudFront → Distributions, open the distribution from the DistributionId output and verify the VPC origin and deployment status:
Your CloudFront distribution and VPC origin; redact the domain and account ID if sharing. The ALB uses the internal scheme and has no public IP. HTTPS terminates at CloudFront, and the template forwards HTTP from CloudFront to the internal ALB; this setup is intended for the lab environment. See the CloudFront VPC origins requirements .

title: Blog 1
content:
Amazon Transcribe vs OpenAI Whisper: Which Speech-to-Text Solution Is Better Suited to Vietnamese? Speech-to-Text (STT) technology is increasingly common, from automatic video captions and meeting transcripts to customer support call analysis. Two notable solutions are Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper. Both convert audio into text, but they differ significantly in their deployment models, capabilities, pricing structures, and operational requirements.
These differences are particularly relevant for Vietnamese, a tonal language with regional accents and frequent mixing of Vietnamese and English technical terms. Choosing the wrong service can lead to low transcription accuracy, unexpected operational costs, or excessive infrastructure maintenance.
This article provides a comprehensive comparison of the two options across speech recognition capabilities, Vietnamese language support, deployment models, cost analysis, practical architectures, evaluation metrics, and real-world decision guidance.
1. Overview of Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper Amazon Transcribe Amazon Transcribe is an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) service from AWS. It converts audio into text without requiring developers to build or operate their own machine learning model.
As a fully managed service, AWS maintains the underlying infrastructure, speech recognition models, scaling, and updates. The application provides audio input and the necessary processing configuration.
Amazon Transcribe offers two main processing modes:
Batch Transcription: Transcribes existing audio recordings stored in Amazon S3. Suitable for offline processing of lectures, interviews, and call center recordings. Streaming Transcription: Transcribes incoming audio with near-real-time results. Suitable for live captioning, virtual assistants, and real-time meeting assistants. Depending on the language, the service also provides features such as Custom Vocabulary, Speaker Diarization, Language Identification, Content Redaction, and Call Analytics.
Its ability to integrate with Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS Step Functions, and other AWS services makes it useful for automated audio-processing workflows without managing servers.
OpenAI Whisper Whisper is an open-source speech recognition model introduced by OpenAI in 2022. It uses a Transformer architecture and was trained on approximately 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask supervised data collected from the web.
Whisper supports multilingual speech transcription, language detection, and translation of speech into English.
It is available in several model sizes, including Tiny, Base, Small, Medium, Large-v1, Large-v2, Large-v3, and Turbo, with different compute requirements and performance trade-offs.
Unlike Amazon Transcribe, the open-source model can run locally or on cloud infrastructure such as Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, or Amazon EKS.
This gives developers control over the runtime environment, model selection, versioning, and data processing. In exchange, they must manage the computing resources, dependencies, model weights, application infrastructure, security patches, and scaling themselves.
Figure 2. OpenAI Whisper’s Transformer encoder-decoder architecture for multilingual speech recognition. Source: OpenAI GitHub.
2. Vietnamese Speech Recognition Capabilities Vietnamese is a tonal language with six tones, rich diacritics, regional accents (Northern, Central, Southern), and frequent code-switching between Vietnamese and English technical terms. Noisy recordings and unclear pronunciation make accurate transcription more difficult.
Vietnamese Support in Amazon Transcribe According to AWS documentation referenced for this post, Amazon Transcribe supports Vietnamese (vi-VN) in both batch and streaming modes.
Custom Vocabulary is useful for adding names, product terms, and domain-specific terminology to improve recognition accuracy for Vietnamese technical conversations.
However, Vietnamese was not supported by Amazon Transcribe’s automatic Language Identification feature in the referenced language support table. Applications processing Vietnamese audio should therefore specify vi-VN explicitly rather than relying on auto-detection.
Custom Language Models and some advanced analysis features were also unavailable for Vietnamese in that language support information at the time of publication.
Vietnamese Support in Whisper Whisper supports Vietnamese through its multilingual models. It can detect the input language automatically or be configured to use a specified language code (vi).
Its diverse audio training data provides a basis for handling various speakers and recording conditions, although the model does not produce perfect results in every setting.
For example, consider the sentence:
“Hôm nay sẽ deploy ứng dụng lên Amazon EC2, sau đó cấu hình Security Group và kết nối với RDS.”
English technical terms such as “deploy”, “Security Group”, and “RDS” may be misrecognized when pronunciation is unclear or background noise is present.
With Amazon Transcribe, Custom Vocabulary is one possible way to improve recognition of technical expressions. With Whisper, developers can experiment with different model sizes (Large-v3 typically performs best) and context prompts where supported.
Without a common benchmark dataset, it would be misleading to claim that either system is consistently more accurate for Vietnamese. A fair comparison should cover Northern, Central, and Southern accents, audio quality (telephony vs. studio), background noise levels, and different speaking scenarios (formal presentations vs. casual conversations).
3. Deployment Cost Comparison Cost matters, particularly for applications that process hundreds or thousands of hours of audio.
Amazon Transcribe Amazon Transcribe uses pay-as-you-go pricing based on the processed audio duration.
Using an illustrative first-tier Standard Transcription rate of USD 0.024 per minute in US East (N. Virginia), processing ten hours of audio would cost approximately USD 14.40.
Actual charges depend on AWS Region, pricing tiers, optional features (such as speaker diarization or content redaction), and additional services such as S3 storage and Lambda invocations.
A key benefit is that the application does not have to keep a GPU server running or manage the ASR model. This can be valuable when workloads are irregular or unpredictable.
OpenAI Whisper The open-source Whisper model has no model license fee, but inference still requires computing resources.
When deployed on Amazon EC2, costs depend on instance type, runtime duration, storage, data transfer, and performance requirements.
Whisper can run on CPUs, but larger models (Large-v2, Large-v3) typically require GPUs for acceptable inference speed. GPUs can speed up inference in many scenarios, at the cost of more expensive infrastructure.
For applications processing just a few recordings each day, keeping a GPU instance online continuously may be inefficient. On the other hand, existing infrastructure or Spot Instances that can be started only when needed may make self-hosting worthwhile.
The open-source model should not be confused with the hosted OpenAI Whisper API. The whisper-1 API is a separately billed service, and OpenAI announced its discontinuation for February 26, 2027. This does not discontinue the open-source Whisper model.
A fair cost comparison therefore needs to include compute, storage, operations, maintenance, scalability, and engineering time—not just a price per audio minute.
Summary Table Factor Amazon Transcribe OpenAI Whisper (self-hosted) Pricing model Pay per audio minute Compute instance cost + engineering time Infrastructure Fully managed by AWS Self-managed on EC2/ECS/EKS GPU required No Recommended for Large models Scaling Automatic Manual or Auto Scaling group Model updates Managed by AWS Manual version management Data residency Configurable AWS Region Full control over deployment location 4. Practical Use Case: Turning Lectures into Text A useful Speech-to-Text application is a service that automatically converts recorded lectures to searchable transcripts. Students can look up key passages, extract information, or generate summaries rather than listening to the entire recording again.
Both Amazon Transcribe and Whisper can support this workflow.
Option A: Amazon Transcribe The architecture can combine Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, and Amazon Transcribe:
A user uploads an audio file to Amazon S3. The upload event triggers AWS Lambda. Lambda starts a Transcription Job with the language code vi-VN. Amazon Transcribe processes the audio and produces the transcript. The transcript is stored in S3 for the application to retrieve. This approach uses managed AWS services and requires no self-hosted speech recognition model.
Option B: Whisper on Amazon EC2 The architecture can combine Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, and Amazon EC2:
An audio recording is uploaded to S3. A processing request is sent to an Amazon SQS queue. An EC2 worker receives the request and downloads the audio. Whisper transcribes the recording into Vietnamese text. The result is saved to Amazon S3. The second option requires direct control of the inference environment, but makes it possible to choose the Whisper version, configure compute resources, and optimize the pipeline.
Either solution could later include automatic lecture summarization using an LLM through Amazon Bedrock.
5. How Should Accuracy Be Evaluated? A few individual recordings are not enough to evaluate a Speech-to-Text system fairly.
A useful test dataset could include:
Recordings of speakers from different Vietnamese regions (Northern, Central, Southern). Clear studio-quality recordings and recordings with background noise. Everyday conversations and conversations containing technical vocabulary. Code-switched Vietnamese-English technical discussions. The same dataset should then be processed by both services and compared against human-verified reference transcripts.
Two common evaluation metrics are:
Word Error Rate (WER): Measures recognition errors at the word level compared with a reference transcript.
Character Error Rate (CER): Measures recognition errors at the character level.
Lower values generally indicate better recognition under the selected metric. For Vietnamese, a consistent text normalization procedure (handling diacritics, case, and punctuation) is important before calculating the scores.
Processing time, cost per audio hour, and operational complexity should also be considered. A small accuracy gain may not justify substantially higher infrastructure costs for every application.
6. When Should Each Solution Be Considered? Amazon Transcribe is a practical option for applications already using AWS, especially when the goal is to deliver a speech transcription feature quickly without maintaining the ML infrastructure.
Its near-real-time Vietnamese streaming support and integration with other AWS services are significant advantages.
Self-hosted Whisper is worth considering for research, custom inference workflows, or environments where direct control of model deployment, versioning, and data handling is important.
However, hardware requirements, model versioning, and ongoing operations should be evaluated carefully before choosing a self-hosted deployment.
7. Conclusion Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper address the same Speech-to-Text problem with different approaches.
Amazon Transcribe provides a managed recognition service, reducing deployment and operations work. The open-source Whisper model offers greater flexibility and control over the runtime and model configuration.
Both support Vietnamese, but comparative accuracy needs to be tested on the same input data rather than assumed.
The right decision depends on transcript quality, cost, performance, scalability, and operational requirements. A useful next step would be to benchmark both solutions against a Vietnamese dataset containing multiple regional accents and recording conditions.

title: Bot and Fargate Runtime
content:
1. Create the bot task definition In CloudShell:
CLUSTER="$(stackout tina-staging ClusterName)" BUCKET="$(stackout tina-staging StagingRecordingsBucket)" aws cloudformation deploy --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name tina-ws-bot --template-file "$TINA_SRC/deploy/aws/ecs-bot.yml" \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM \ --parameter-overrides "ClusterName=$CLUSTER" "BotImage=$(image bot)" \ "BotRepositoryArn=$(repoarn bot)" "InvocationBucket=$BUCKET" ProbeInvocation=false This template creates the bot task definition and IAM roles. Bot tasks are launched on demand by Runtime when a meeting is requested; having no always-on bot service is expected.
2. Deploy Runtime VPC_ID="$(stackout tina-staging VpcId)" APP_SUBNETS="$(stackout tina-staging AppSubnetIds)" APP_SG="$(stackout tina-ws-data AppSecurityGroupId)" aws cloudformation deploy --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name tina-ws-runtime --template-file "$TINA_SRC/deploy/aws/staging-runtime.yml" \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM \ --parameter-overrides "ClusterName=$CLUSTER" "VpcId=$VPC_ID" "AppSubnetIds=$APP_SUBNETS" \ "AppSecurityGroupId=$APP_SG" "RuntimeImage=$(image runtime)" \ "RuntimeRepositoryArn=$(repoarn runtime)" \ "RuntimeTaskRoleArn=$(stackout tina-ws-bot RuntimeTaskRoleArn)" \ "BotTaskDefinitionArn=$(stackout tina-ws-bot BotTaskDefinitionArn)" \ "BotImage=$(image bot)" "InvocationBucket=$BUCKET" \ "ValkeyHost=$(stackout tina-ws-data ValkeyHost)" \ "ValkeySecretArn=$(stackout tina-ws-data ValkeySecretArn)" Wait for the stack to succeed. This template also creates the tina-staging.local Cloud Map private namespace in your VPC; do not create a duplicate namespace in the same VPC. Retrieve the namespace ID for the subsequent stacks:
NAMESPACE_ID="$(aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name tina-ws-runtime --logical-resource-id DiscoveryNamespace \ --query 'StackResourceDetail.PhysicalResourceId' --output text)" printf 'Namespace ID: %s\n' "$NAMESPACE_ID" Go to ECS → Clusters, select the cluster from ClusterName, and verify that the Runtime service has a Running task. After deploying core and terminal, return here to capture the full service list:
ECS services after deploying Runtime, core, and terminal, showing desired and running tasks. Open the Runtime task → Containers and inspect its status; capture only sections that do not expose tokens or sensitive environment variables:
Runtime task and container status; redact environment variables and sensitive details. If the task does not reach Running, check Deployments and events, CloudWatch logs, Fargate quotas, NAT egress routing, ECR permissions, and image architecture.

title: NAT, routes and endpoint
content:
1. Create the NAT Gateway with the CloudFormation CLI The foundation stack already attached an Internet Gateway to the VPC. In CloudShell, run:
PUBLIC_SUBNETS="$(stackout tina-staging PublicSubnetIds)" APP_ROUTES="$(stackout tina-staging AppRouteTableIds)" IFS=, read -r PUBLIC_A PUBLIC_B <<< "$PUBLIC_SUBNETS" IFS=, read -r ROUTE_A ROUTE_B <<< "$APP_ROUTES" aws cloudformation deploy --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name tina-ws-egress --template-file "$TINA_SRC/deploy/aws/staging-egress.yml" \ --parameter-overrides "PublicSubnetId=$PUBLIC_A" "AppRouteTableA=$ROUTE_A" "AppRouteTableB=$ROUTE_B" Verify the Internet Gateway attached to the VPC under VPC → Internet gateways:
VPC Internet Gateway in the attached state. Verify the NAT Gateway under VPC → NAT gateways; the stack must be CREATE_COMPLETE and the NAT Gateway Available:
NAT Gateway created by the egress stack, with status Available. 2. Verify Routes and the S3 Endpoint In VPC → Route tables, inspect the app route tables: the 0.0.0.0/0 route points to the NAT Gateway. The public route table points to the Internet Gateway, and the data subnets have no default Internet route. Both app route tables include the S3 gateway endpoint.
App subnet route table with a default route through the NAT Gateway. Under VPC → Endpoints, locate the endpoint ID matching the S3EndpointId output from the foundation stack:
S3 gateway endpoint and its associated app route tables. Security groups for the application and database will be created by the data stack in a later section. You do not need to create them manually now.
Using a single NAT Gateway shared across two AZs reduces resource count, but introduces a single-AZ dependency and may incur cross-AZ data transfer charges. See the AWS CloudFront VPC origins documentation for Internet Gateway and available IPv4 address requirements.

title: Prerequisites
content:
1. Account and Region Use an isolated AWS account for the lab with permissions to create CloudFormation stacks, IAM roles, VPC, EC2, ECS, ECR, RDS, ElastiCache, S3, CloudFront, WAF, Secrets Manager, and CloudWatch resources. Do not use a production account. Sign in to the AWS Console and select US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1 in the top-right corner. CloudFront and WAF for CloudFront use global configuration, and the WAF API for CloudFront requires us-east-1. AWS Console with Region us-east-1 selected. In Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget, create a cost budget with your chosen threshold and email address. Confirm the alert email following the AWS instructions. A budget only sends alerts; it does not automatically stop resources. Budget and alert threshold for your lab account; mask your email and account ID. In Service Quotas, check your quotas for Fargate On-Demand, EC2 Graviton, Elastic IPs, and RDS. Each bot requires 4 vCPU / 8 GiB; core uses 2 vCPU, VieGem uses 2 vCPU, plus runtime and terminal. Leave enough headroom for replacement tasks during ECS redeployments. Note that AWS Free Plan accounts enforce a strict cap on the number of RDS instances—if other RDS instances are already running, creating PostgreSQL may fail with ServiceLimitExceeded. NAT Gateway, public IPv4 addresses, Fargate, RDS, Valkey, ALB, WAF, S3, ECR, the builder instance, and CloudFront may incur charges. Check the AWS Pricing Calculator for your Region and expected runtime. This workshop is not guaranteed to stay within the AWS Free Tier.
Fast Path (Recommended): If you choose the single-file CloudFormation deployment with prebuilt ARM64 images from GHCR, once you complete Section 1 above, simply open AWS CloudShell (us-east-1) and jump straight to 5.4A Single CloudFormation Deployment (you can skip Sections 2 and 3 below).
2. Source Code and Templates (for the multi-stack path 5.3 → 5.4) This workshop uses commit 8a2b79e884bc0833f9075d4e795b20d347cef9c2 on main in the TINA repository , which includes the full ECS backend, VieGem ASR, Voice, Bedrock (amazon.nova-lite-v1:0), Amazon SES (staging-ses.yml), and CloudWatch Dashboard/Alarms (staging-workspace-s3-monitoring.yml).
On your local machine, download the source ZIP at this commit and extract it. Note the deploy/aws/ directory because a Console step will ask you to upload foundation.yml (if you choose the 5-command quick path in 5.4A , you do not need to download the ZIP or build Docker images yourself). You do not need to copy any secrets from the author’s machine.
3. Open AWS CloudShell In the Console, click the CloudShell icon and confirm that the Region is us-east-1. All bash commands from here on run in CloudShell unless a page explicitly states to run them in EC2 Session Manager.
In CloudShell, download the same template revision and define helper functions for reading stack outputs:
mkdir -p "$HOME/tina-workshop" cat > "$HOME/tina-workshop/env.sh" <<'EOF' export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 export AWS_PAGER='' export TINA_REV=8a2b79e884bc0833f9075d4e795b20d347cef9c2 export TINA_SRC="$HOME/tina-workshop/TINA-${TINA_REV}" export TINA_ACCOUNT="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)" export TINA_TAG=ws-v1 stackout() { aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$AWS_REGION" --stack-name "$1" \ --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='$2'].OutputValue | [0]" --output text } repoarn() { aws ecr describe-repositories --region "$AWS_REGION" --repository-names "tina-staging/$1" \ --query 'repositories[0].repositoryArn' --output text } image() { local d d="$(aws ecr describe-images --region "$AWS_REGION" --repository-name "tina-staging/$1" \ --image-ids "imageTag=$TINA_TAG" --query 'imageDetails[0].imageDigest' --output text)" || return 1 printf '%s.dkr.ecr.%s.amazonaws.com/tina-staging/%s@%s' "$TINA_ACCOUNT" "$AWS_REGION" "$1" "$d" } EOF grep -q 'tina-workshop/env.sh' ~/.bashrc || echo 'source "$HOME/tina-workshop/env.sh"' >> ~/.bashrc source "$HOME/tina-workshop/env.sh" curl -fL "https://github.com/poor-frog/TINA/archive/${TINA_REV}.zip" -o "$HOME/tina-workshop/source.zip" unzip -q -o "$HOME/tina-workshop/source.zip" -d "$HOME/tina-workshop" These commands persist your variables and helper functions in ~/tina-workshop/env.sh (auto-loaded by ~/.bashrc), so even if CloudShell disconnects and reconnects during sections 5.3 → 5.4, you will not lose $TINA_SRC, $TINA_ACCOUNT, $TINA_TAG, or stackout. Subsequent steps use the image tag ws-v1; if you need to rebuild after a partial push, choose a new tag and use it consistently in both EC2 and CloudShell because ECR repositories are configured with immutable tags.
