title: Proposal
content:
TINA – AI Meeting Assistant on AWS A Containerized AWS Solution for Real-Time Meeting Transcription, Notes and Follow-ups Group: KimThiem
Full Name Student ID University Email Trần Kiến Quốc SE190250 FPT University quockientran100@gmail.com Hoàng Đình Quang SE192303 FPT University quanghd023@gmail.com Lê Hoài Thanh Quang SE190062 FPT University lethanhquang094@gmail.com Thái Việt Nam SE192065 FPT University vnam27122005@gmail.com 1. Executive Summary TINA is an AI meeting assistant built by a four-person team during the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) internship. A meeting bot joins Google Meet, transcribes the conversation in real time (Vietnamese first, with English and bilingual views), produces live notes and a summary, and lets participants ask questions about the meeting (“Ask TINA”), including spoken replies through a wake word. When the meeting ends, every known attendee receives a follow-up email linking to the saved summary and recording.
The platform runs on AWS in us-east-1. Containerized services run on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind CloudFront, AWS WAF and an Application Load Balancer. Google OAuth (integrated via NextAuth) handles sign-in. Amazon RDS and Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey/Redis) store transcripts and live state, Amazon S3 stores recordings, Amazon Bedrock powers summaries and the meeting agent, and Amazon SES delivers follow-up emails.
Objectives & Scope Pilot audience: Internal team of about 10 users holding ≈5 meetings/week (≈20 meeting-hours/month). Technical objective: Build a secure, containerized AWS architecture (2-AZ VPC, private subnets, KMS, Secrets Manager) delivering real-time Vietnamese transcription and automated post-meeting notes and follow-ups. Deployment scope: Core online meeting workflows on Google Meet, AI summaries/notes, voice assistant, and cost-optimized operation within internship AWS credits (Single-AZ data tier, not HA production). 2. Problem Statement Teams lose information in meetings. Someone has to take notes by hand, so decisions, owners and deadlines are missed or recorded inconsistently. People who join late or miss the meeting have no reliable record to catch up from.
In addition, most commercial meeting assistants present three major drawbacks for teams in Vietnam:
High per-seat pricing: Subscription costs grow rapidly when rolled out across an entire team. Weak Vietnamese support: Transcription accuracy drops on Vietnamese speech and mixed Vietnamese–English technical terms. Lack of data ownership: Internal meeting recordings and transcripts are stored on third-party servers outside the team’s control. 3. Proposed Solution & Benefits The Solution TINA sends a bot into the meeting through a headless browser (Playwright). The bot streams the meeting audio to a self-hosted speech-to-text service (VieGem, tuned for Vietnamese). Finalized transcript segments are stored in Amazon RDS, and live updates are pushed through Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey/Redis) to the web app. An agent service uses Amazon Bedrock to keep notes and a summary current, translate transcripts for the English/bilingual view, and answer questions about the selected meeting. A TTS service (VieNeu) lets TINA answer aloud when someone calls its wake word. After the meeting, recordings are saved to Amazon S3 and Amazon SES emails each attendee a follow-up with links whose access is bound to the recipient’s signed-in account.
Key features:
Meeting bot for Google Meet; live transcript with Vietnamese, English and bilingual views. Live notes, end-of-meeting summary and transcript search. “Ask TINA” agent with meeting context, plus wake-word and spoken replies. Post-meeting follow-up email with recipient-bound summary and recording links. Google OAuth sign-in (NextAuth); secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, encryption with AWS KMS. Benefits and Return on Investment (ROI) Time saved: Removes manual note-taking and follow-up writing, saving roughly 15–30 minutes per meeting for the note-taker; at ~5 meetings/week that is 5–10 hours per month for the pilot team. Better follow-through: Decisions and action items are captured in a searchable record and sent to every attendee. Data ownership: All meeting data, recordings and models stay inside the team’s own AWS account. Learning value: Gives the team hands-on experience with ECS/Fargate, networking, managed databases, generative AI on Bedrock and CI/CD — a reusable foundation for future AI products. Cost: About $137/month on-demand in us-east-1 (Fargate ARM64 & Valkey) with the full architecture running 24/7 (see section 6). With off-hours scale-down it fits within the team’s AWS credits for the internship and pilot period, much lower than per-seat SaaS licenses for 10 users. 4. Technical Architecture & Implementation Solution Architecture TINA uses a containerized architecture on Amazon ECS (AWS Fargate) inside a VPC across two Availability Zones in us-east-1. Public traffic enters through CloudFront and AWS WAF, then an Application Load Balancer. All application tasks run in private subnets. Data stores sit in separate private data subnets, and outbound traffic (meeting platforms, Google OAuth) leaves through a NAT Gateway.
Request and data flow (numbers match the diagram):
The user opens TINA through CloudFront (protected by WAF) and signs in with Google OAuth. CloudFront forwards requests to the VPC through the Internet Gateway. Traffic reaches the Application Load Balancer. The ALB routes HTTPS traffic to the Web serving task (Next.js terminal, API, WebSocket gateway). When a meeting starts, the Web task launches a Bot task (Playwright). The bot joins Google Meet through the NAT Gateway over HTTPS/WebRTC. The bot streams audio to the STT (VieGem) task (7.1) and stores recordings in Amazon S3 (7.2). Transcript segments are written to RDS and live state to ElastiCache. The Web and Bot tasks call the Agent task for notes, summaries, translation and Ask TINA. The Agent calls Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference. Live updates flow from ElastiCache/RDS back to the Web task (11.1); the TTS (VieNeu) task speaks agent replies into the meeting through the bot (11.2). After the meeting, the Web task sends a follow-up email through Amazon SES to the participants. CI/CD: GitHub Actions builds container images, pushes them to Amazon ECR, and ECS rolls out new task revisions. CloudWatch collects logs, metrics and alarms for the ALB, ECS tasks, RDS, ElastiCache and Bedrock.
AWS Services Used Amazon CloudFront + AWS WAF: Global entry point, TLS, caching of static assets and protection against common web attacks. Amazon VPC, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway: Network isolation with public, private and private-data subnets across 2 AZs; controlled outbound access. Application Load Balancer: HTTPS/WebSocket routing to the Web task with health checks. Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate: Runs five service groups — Web serving, Bot (Playwright), STT (VieGem), TTS (VieNeu), Agent — without managing servers. Amazon ECR: Private registry for container images. Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL): Meetings, transcripts, notes, users and settings. Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey/Redis): Live transcript streams, pub/sub and short-lived state. Amazon S3: Meeting recordings and exported artifacts. Amazon Bedrock: LLM for notes, summaries, translation and the meeting agent. Amazon SES: Post-meeting follow-up emails. IAM, AWS Secrets Manager, AWS KMS: Least-privilege task roles, secret storage (DB password, OAuth client secret, service tokens) and encryption keys. Amazon CloudWatch: Logs, metrics, dashboards and alarms. AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets: Cost tracking and budget alerts. Component Design Client: Web app (TINA Terminal) and Chrome extension; users sign in with Google OAuth (NextAuth). Edge layer: CloudFront + WAF in front of the ALB; only HTTPS is exposed publicly. Web serving task: UI, REST API, WebSocket gateway for live transcripts, meeting orchestration and email dispatch. Bot task: One Playwright browser per meeting; captures audio per participant channel and plays TTS audio back into the meeting. Speech tasks: STT (VieGem) converts audio windows to draft/confirmed transcript segments; TTS (VieNeu) generates spoken replies. Agent task: Builds meeting context and calls Bedrock for notes, summaries, bilingual translation and Ask TINA answers. Data layer: RDS for durable data, ElastiCache for real-time streams, S3 for recordings — all in private data subnets, encrypted with KMS. Operations: GitHub Actions → ECR → ECS deployment; CloudWatch monitoring; Budgets alerts. Implementation Phases Research and architecture design (Weeks 1–6): Learn core AWS services through FCAJ labs; study the TINA codebase (meeting bot, ASR, agent); draw the AWS architecture. Cost estimation and feasibility check (Weeks 7–8): Estimate costs with the AWS Pricing Calculator; test Bedrock models and Vietnamese ASR quality; adjust sizing to fit the credit budget. Architecture refinement (Weeks 8–9): Containerize every service, move secrets to Secrets Manager, split networking into public/private/data subnets and define IAM roles per task. Development, testing and deployment (Weeks 9–12): Build features (voice assistant, wake word, post-meeting email, bilingual translation), set up CI/CD with GitHub Actions and ECR, deploy to ECS Fargate, run end-to-end tests with real meetings and tune costs. Technical Requirements Application: TypeScript/Next.js (web), Python (meeting API, agent), Playwright (bot), ARM64 Docker images for every service; pnpm/turbo monorepo. Speech: VieGem STT and VieNeu TTS models served over authenticated HTTP inside the VPC; model artifacts stored in S3/ECR. AWS: ECS Fargate task definitions and services, ALB target groups with health checks, RDS PostgreSQL, ElastiCache Valkey/Redis, S3 buckets with encryption and lifecycle rules, Google OAuth via Secrets Manager, Bedrock model access, SES verified domain. Security: Least-privilege IAM task roles, Secrets Manager for credentials, KMS encryption at rest, TLS in transit, security groups that only allow ALB → Web and internal service-to-service traffic. DevOps: GitHub Actions for build/test, image push to ECR and ECS deployment; CloudWatch logs and alarms. 5. Timeline & Milestones Week Team Member Planned Tasks Week 7 All Members Kickoff meeting, agree on MVP scope (bot, live transcript, notes/summary, Ask TINA, follow-up email), finalize the architecture diagram, set up the shared Git repo and IAM accounts. Trần Kiến Quốc Analyse the voice flow (wake word → Agent → TTS) and the post-meeting email requirements. Thái Việt Nam Finalize architecture documentation, plan the VPC/subnets across 2 AZs and draft IAM policies. Hoàng Đình Quang Evaluate Vietnamese STT (VieGem) accuracy and latency on sample meeting recordings. Lê Hoài Thanh Quang Test Bedrock models for notes/summaries and estimate costs with the AWS Pricing Calculator. Week 8 All Members Agree on contracts between Web, Bot, STT, TTS and Agent (transcript segments, events, APIs); containerize every service. Trần Kiến Quốc Containerize the TTS (VieNeu) service and set up GitHub Actions to build and push images to ECR. Thái Việt Nam Provision VPC, NAT Gateway, ALB, ECS cluster, CloudFront + WAF and Google OAuth sign-in configuration. Hoàng Đình Quang Containerize the Bot (Playwright) and STT services and write their Fargate task definitions. Lê Hoài Thanh Quang Set up RDS PostgreSQL, ElastiCache Valkey/Redis and the S3 recordings bucket with encryption. Week 9 All Members Peer code review; integrate the Bot → STT → RDS/ElastiCache → Web live transcript flow. Trần Kiến Quốc Build the voice assistant and wake word; play TTS replies into the meeting through the bot. Thái Việt Nam Configure Secrets Manager, KMS, least-privilege IAM task roles and security groups. Hoàng Đình Quang Capture audio per participant channel, tune endpointing and add the bilingual transcript view. Lê Hoài Thanh Quang Build the Agent: live notes, end-of-meeting summary and Ask TINA via Bedrock. Week 10 All Members End-to-end tests with real Google Meet meetings and bug fixes. Trần Kiến Quốc Post-meeting follow-up email via Amazon SES with recipient-bound summary/recording links. Thái Việt Nam CloudWatch dashboards/alarms and AWS Budgets cost alerts. Hoàng Đình Quang Stabilize Google Meet audio capture, improve speaker attribution, and reduce STT latency. Lê Hoài Thanh Quang Tune prompts, add transcript search and track Bedrock token cost. Week 11 All Members Review test results, find bottlenecks and optimize costs. Trần Kiến Quốc Regression tests for the voice, wake word and email flows; keep CI green. Thái Việt Nam Off-hours scale-down, Fargate Spot, VPC endpoints; basic security audit (WAF, IAM). Hoàng Đình Quang Load test concurrent meetings and tune Fargate CPU/memory for Bot and STT. Lê Hoài Thanh Quang Evaluate notes/summary quality in Vietnamese and English; configure a fallback model. Week 12 All Members Full system run, record the demo video, complete documentation and presentation, and submit. 6. Budget Estimation Estimates use on-demand prices in us-east-1 (US East – N. Virginia) via the AWS Pricing Calculator for the pilot workload: ≈10 users, ≈5 meetings/week of about 1 hour (≈20 meeting-hours/month). Always-on services run 24/7; meeting services (Bot, STT, TTS) run only while a meeting is active.
Infrastructure Cost Table Category Service Sizing / Usage Monthly Cost (USD) Compute (ECS Fargate ARM64) Web serving 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB, 24/7 14.42 Agent 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB, 24/7 14.42 Bot – Playwright 1 vCPU, 2 GB, 20 h 0.79 STT – VieGem 2 vCPU, 4 GB, 20 h 1.58 TTS – VieNeu 1 vCPU, 2 GB, 20 h 0.79 Networking Application Load Balancer 1 ALB, low LCU 18.00 NAT Gateway 1 gateway, ≈10 GB processed 33.30 Public IPv4 addresses 3 addresses 10.95 Amazon CloudFront Mostly within free tier 1.00 Data Amazon RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.micro, Single-AZ, 20 GB gp3 14.00 Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey) cache.t4g.micro 9.34 Amazon S3 ≈10 GB recordings + requests 0.33 AI & Messaging Amazon Bedrock amazon.nova-lite-v1:0 + fallback (notes, summaries, translation, Q&A) ≈3.00 Amazon SES ≈200 emails 0.01 Security & Operations AWS WAF 1 Web ACL, 3 rules 8.00 AWS Secrets Manager 5 secrets 2.00 AWS KMS 1 customer managed key 1.00 Amazon CloudWatch ≈5 GB logs, alarms 3.50 Amazon ECR ≈10 GB images 1.00 Total Full architecture (24/7) ≈$1,649 / 12 months ≈$137.43 Cost optimization: Stopping the Web/Agent tasks, RDS and ElastiCache outside working hours (~10 h/day, weekdays) and removing WAF in the development environment brings the demo/pilot cost to about $70–80/month. Further options: Fargate Spot for the Bot/STT/TTS tasks, VPC endpoints for S3/ECR to reduce NAT data charges, and S3 lifecycle rules that move old recordings to cheaper storage classes. AWS Budgets alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% of the monthly limit.
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Risk Description Impact Probability Cost overrun NAT Gateway, ALB and always-on tasks High Medium Vietnamese ASR accuracy Regional accents, noise, mixed English terms High Medium Meeting platform changes Google Meet UI updates or bot blocking High Medium Real-time latency Audio → transcript → notes pipeline Medium Medium Data privacy Internal meeting recordings and transcripts High Low Bedrock quota / availability Quota limits or model outage Medium Low Mitigation Strategies Cost: AWS Budgets alerts, Cost Explorer reviews, off-hours scale-down, Fargate Spot for meeting tasks, run meeting tasks only on demand. ASR accuracy: Use VieGem tuned for Vietnamese, endpointing that confirms stable text, measure accuracy on recorded test meetings. Platform changes: Per-platform capture adapters, regression tests on Playwright flows, quick image rollout through CI/CD. Latency: Keep STT inside the VPC, stream partial results, use a fast/low-cost Bedrock model for live notes. Privacy: Consent notice before recording, Google OAuth (NextAuth) authentication, recipient-bound links, KMS encryption, private subnets, least-privilege IAM, retention rules on S3. Bedrock: Request quota in advance, keep a fallback model configured. Contingency Plans If the budget is close to the limit, scale the ECS services to zero and stop RDS/ElastiCache; keep only S3 and the database snapshot. If a deployment fails, roll back to the previous ECS task definition revision. If live transcription is unavailable, keep the bot recording to S3 and transcribe after the meeting. If Bedrock is unavailable, deliver the transcript and recording links without the AI summary. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements Meetings are transcribed and summarized automatically, in real time, with Vietnamese as a first-class language. Attendees receive notes and recordings right after the meeting; no manual note-taking. A secure, monitored, containerized deployment on AWS with automated CI/CD. Each service scales independently; meeting tasks run only when needed. Current Limitations Meeting platform: The current release is tested and tuned on Google Meet only; the Playwright bot can be affected by Google Meet UI updates or room admission policies that restrict guest participants. Pilot-scale infrastructure: Amazon RDS and ElastiCache run Single-AZ to keep lab costs low (no Multi-AZ HA / auto-failover yet); concurrent voice rooms are capped for pilot sizing (MaxRooms=3). ASR model licensing: VieGem is released under a non-commercial license (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0) and must be swapped for a commercially licensed ASR model for commercial deployment. Authentication & External integrations: Currently supports Google OAuth only (no enterprise SAML/OIDC SSO yet) and does not yet sync action items bidirectionally to Jira, Notion, or Slack. Future Improvements & Roadmap Additional meeting platforms: Build and validate capture adapters for Zoom and Microsoft Teams alongside Google Meet. Production readiness: Upgrade RDS/ElastiCache to Multi-AZ, configure ECS Fargate Auto Scaling, and implement automated backup/Disaster Recovery drills. Enhanced speech & AI quality: Improve speaker diarization, support pluggable commercial/multilingual ASR models, and build automated LLM summary evaluation benchmarks. Workspace ecosystem & governance: Two-way sync of Action Items with Notion, Jira, Slack, and Microsoft 365, plus enterprise SSO (SAML/OIDC) and team role-based access control (RBAC).

title: Blog 2
content:
From Meeting Transcripts to Notion Tasks: When DynamoDB Streams, Lambda, and Bedrock Work Together Having a complete transcript after a meeting does not necessarily solve the follow-up problem. A transcript might contain thousands of words, while the most useful information is often much simpler: Who is responsible for which task? What is the deadline? Which action items still need attention?
Manually listening to recordings, reading through long transcripts, deciding what needs to be done, writing it down, and creating tasks in a project management tool is time-consuming and error-prone. Important items get forgotten, deadlines are missed, and context is lost between the meeting and the task tracker.
One practical approach is to combine Amazon DynamoDB Streams, AWS Lambda, and Amazon Bedrock to extract action items automatically and synchronize them with Notion. This post walks through the architecture, implementation considerations, a Python code example, idempotency strategies, human-in-the-loop confirmation, cost considerations, and how to extend the pattern to other tools.
1. How Does the Architecture Work? Imagine that someone says during a meeting:
“Lan will finish the login API by October 30.”
After the meeting ends, the system can follow this workflow:
Amazon DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams The backend updates the meeting status to COMPLETED in DynamoDB. DynamoDB Streams captures the data change, and AWS Lambda can be configured to process the stream event.
The useful separation here is that the backend does not need to invoke the entire AI workflow directly. Post-meeting analysis can run independently, and the main application remains responsive.
AWS Lambda Lambda acts as the coordinator. It receives the stream event, retrieves the corresponding transcript from Amazon S3, and prepares the content for AI processing.
Instead of copying a long transcript into Notion, the Lambda function asks a model available through Amazon Bedrock to identify relevant action items.
Amazon Bedrock The language model turns conversational content into structured data. For example:
Task: Complete the login API Assignee: Lan Deadline: October 30 Source: The relevant transcript segment After receiving the response, Lambda validates the data and calls the Notion API to create an item in a task database.
Why This Design Works Event-driven: No polling. The pipeline starts automatically when meeting metadata changes in DynamoDB. Serverless: No EC2 instances to manage. You pay only for the compute and API calls you actually use. Decoupled: Transcript storage, AI extraction, and task creation are separate concerns. You can replace Bedrock with another model, or Notion with another task tool, without rewriting the whole pipeline. Observable: Each step emits logs and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch, making failures easy to debug. 2. How It Works Step by Step Step 1: Meeting Metadata Lands in DynamoDB When a meeting finishes, an item is written (or updated) in a DynamoDB table called Meetings:
meeting_id (PK) status transcript_s3_url created_at mtg-2026-10-28-001 completed s3://meeting-transcripts/mtg-001.txt 2026-10-28T10:00:00Z The status field moves from pending to completed. DynamoDB Streams captures this change.
Step 2: Lambda Extracts Action Items with Bedrock A Lambda function (process-meeting-transcript) is triggered by the stream. It:
Reads the meeting_id and transcript_s3_url from the stream record. Downloads the transcript from S3. Calls Amazon Bedrock with a prompt such as: You are an assistant that extracts action items from meeting transcripts.
Transcript: {{transcript}}
Return a JSON array of action items. Each item must have: title, description, assignee, due_date, priority. Only include items that are clearly actionable. Ignore general discussion.
Parses the JSON response from Bedrock. Step 3: Human Confirmation Before creating tasks in Notion, the extracted action items are paused for review. Options include:
Storing proposed tasks in a ProposedTasks DynamoDB table with status = pending_review. Sending a notification (Slack, email, or internal dashboard) with the proposed tasks and Approve/Reject buttons. Only writing to Notion after an approver marks the item as approved. Step 4: Create Tasks in Notion Once confirmed, a Lambda function calls the Notion API (POST https://api.notion.com/v1/pages) to create a page in the Notion database:
Title: Action item title Assignee: Person responsible Due date: When it should be completed Priority: High / Medium / Low Related meeting: Link back to the original meeting record Step 5: Idempotency To avoid creating duplicate tasks if the Lambda is retried or the stream event is delivered twice:
Each proposed task set is stored with a unique meeting_id + batch_id key. Before writing to Notion, the function checks whether tasks for this meeting_id already exist in the ProposedTasks table. Notion page creation records the notion_page_id back to DynamoDB so the same meeting is not processed again. Figure 2. DynamoDB stream shards and AWS Lambda event processing. Source: AWS Database Blog.
3. Example: Lambda Handler (Python) import json import boto3 import os from botocore.exceptions import ClientError s3 = boto3.client("s3") bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime") dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb") MODEL_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_MODEL_ID", "anthropic.claude-3-sonnet-20240229-v1:0") NOTION_DATABASE_ID = os.environ["NOTION_DATABASE_ID"] NOTION_API_KEY = os.environ["NOTION_API_KEY"] PROPOSED_TABLE = os.environ["PROPOSED_TASKS_TABLE"] def extract_action_items(transcript: str) -> list: prompt = f"""Extract action items from this meeting transcript. Return ONLY a JSON array. Each item: {{"title": "...", "description": "...", "assignee": "...", "due_date": "...", "priority": "High|Medium|Low"}} Transcript: {transcript}""" response = bedrock.invoke_model( modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 1000, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}] }) ) result = json.loads(response["body"].read()) return json.loads(result["content"][0]["text"]) def save_proposed_tasks(meeting_id: str, items: list): table = dynamodb.Table(PROPOSED_TABLE) table.put_item(Item={ "meeting_id": meeting_id, "status": "pending_review", "items": items, "created_at": json.dumps({"__type": "timestamp", "iso": str(__import__("datetime").datetime.utcnow())}) }) def already_processed(meeting_id: str) -> bool: table = dynamodb.Table(PROPOSED_TABLE) resp = table.get_item(Key={"meeting_id": meeting_id}) return "Item" in resp def lambda_handler(event, context): for record in event["Records"]: if record["eventName"] not in ("INSERT", "MODIFY"): continue meeting_id = record["dynamodb"]["Keys"]["meeting_id"]["S"] status = record["dynamodb"]["NewImage"].get("status", {}).get("S") s3_url = record["dynamodb"]["NewImage"].get("transcript_s3_url", {}).get("S") if status != "completed" or not s3_url: continue # Idempotency check if already_processed(meeting_id): continue bucket, key = parse_s3_url(s3_url) transcript = s3.get_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)["Body"].read().decode("utf-8") items = extract_action_items(transcript) # Pause for human confirmation before writing to Notion save_proposed_tasks(meeting_id, items) # After confirmation (separate step), call create_notion_tasks(items) return {"statusCode": 200} 4. Idempotency and Human Confirmation Concern How it is handled Duplicate processing DynamoDB table stores processed_meeting_ids; Lambda checks before creating Notion tasks. Stream redelivery Same meeting_id produces the same proposed tasks; Notion creation is gated behind confirmation. Wrong task created Human review step lets an approver edit or reject items before they reach Notion. Partial failure Proposed tasks are stored in DynamoDB first; Notion creation is a separate, retryable step. LLM hallucination Fields not clearly supported by the transcript remain empty rather than being inferred. 5. Cost Considerations Amazon S3: Pay per GB stored and per request. Transcripts are small text files, so cost is negligible. DynamoDB: Pay per read/write request and storage. Ideal for lightweight meeting metadata. AWS Lambda: Pay per invocation and duration. Short Python functions keep cost low. Amazon Bedrock: Pay per input/output token processed by the model. Long transcripts cost more; consider summarizing very long transcripts before sending to Bedrock. Notion API: Free tier is available for small teams; paid plans for higher limits. 6. Extending the Pattern The same architecture can be extended to:
Jira, Asana, Trello, or ClickUp: Replace the Notion API call with the respective task tool API. Email transcripts: Replace S3 + DynamoDB with an SES inbound email handler. Call center transcripts: Replace meeting audio with contact center recordings from Amazon Connect. Scheduled reports: Add a weekly Lambda that scans all pending_review items and sends a summary email. 7. Conclusion This architecture turns meeting transcripts into structured, trackable work without manual copy-paste. By combining DynamoDB Streams, AWS Lambda, Amazon Bedrock, and the Notion API, you get a serverless pipeline that:
Starts automatically when a meeting ends. Extracts action items using generative AI. Keeps humans in the loop before tasks are created. Avoids duplicates with idempotency checks. The same pattern can be extended to other document sources (email, support tickets, call center transcripts) and other task destinations (Jira, Asana, Trello, or a custom database).
References AWS – DynamoDB Streams and Lambda Triggers Amazon Bedrock – Structured Outputs Notion – Create a Page API AWS Lambda – Documentation Bài viết đã đăng trên AWS Study Group: https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2318521822246110/?rdid=ZaQ8iG8gfsmGlEWb#

title: Event 2
content:
Event Takeaways: “AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026: HCMC Watch Party” Event Objectives Catch up on emerging trends in Cloud Computing, Artificial Intelligence and Agentic AI. Learn how AWS and enterprises apply AI Agents to system development, modernization and operations. Catch up on practical content from the Builders x AI track, focused on AI-driven software development. Understand the role of AI across Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) stages such as coding, security, deployment and troubleshooting. Study frameworks, platforms and technologies supporting AI Agent development such as LangGraph, Strands, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and MCP Server. Gain additional perspectives on Data Foundation, Cloud Modernization and AWS Local Zone when building modern systems. Network, exchange ideas and connect with the AWS Builders community, developers, solution architects and Cloud & AI enthusiasts in HCMC. Speakers The event brought together representatives from the Government, AWS, tech enterprises, partners and the builders community. Notable speakers and representatives included:
Mr. Pham Duc Long – Deputy Minister of Science and Technology. Ms. Jennifer Wicks – U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam. Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon.com. Mr. Eric Yeo – General Director of AWS Vietnam. Dr. Jens Lottner – Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Techcombank. Ms. Mai Le – Director of Product Management, Katalon. Dung Luong Tien – AWS Student Builder Group UTC, speaker of “Don’t use a Ferrari to Get Pho” (DEV303). Nguyen Duc Manh – Program Manager, AWS Student Builder Group UTC, speaker of “Agent Harness & Agent Framework: Strands, LangGraph, Bedrock AgentCore” (DEV203). The event also featured:
AWS Solution Architects and Senior Engineers. Experts and CTOs from Renova Cloud. Technology experts from Cloud Kinetics. Representatives from VIB, VPBank, Trusting Social and Green SM. Solution consulting experts from SoftwareOne. At the HCMC hub, keynotes and technical sessions of AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 were followed through the HCMC Watch Party at AWS Office HCM, combined with discussion and networking activities with the AWS Builders community in the southern region.
Key Highlights Opening Keynote Updates on Cloud and AI development trends. The role of Agentic AI Systems in enterprise modernization and transformation. Additional perspectives on digital infrastructure, Data Foundation and enterprise AI strategies. How AWS helps enterprises build and deploy AI workloads on Cloud. Building Software Like Never Before with Agentic AI The role of Agentic AI in software development. AI Agents can help developers perform many tasks and workflows instead of just answering single questions. Additional perspectives on taking AI Agents from experimentation to real-world production. Recognized the potential of Agentic AI in automating repetitive work in software development. From Sprints to AI-Native Delivery: TCBS’ Transformation of SDLC The journey from traditional software development to AI-Native Delivery. AI can be integrated into many different stages of the Software Development Lifecycle. Practical perspectives on applying AI in enterprise environments and large systems. The shift from AI-assisted development to AI-driven development. AWS Security Agent: Proactive AppSec from Design to Deployment How AI is applied to Application Security (AppSec). Security can be introduced early at the design stage instead of only being checked after completion. AI can help developers detect security issues from design through deployment. Recognized the importance of combining AI with security in application development. Tackling Anti-patterns with AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) Issues and anti-patterns that can arise when bringing AI into software development. The concept of AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC). Using AI effectively requires clear workflows, scope and control mechanisms. AI should not be fully depended upon; automation must be combined with human validation. Supercharging AI Coding with MCP Servers and Your Knowledge Servers The role of MCP Servers in AI Coding. MCP helps AI connect to tools, data and external knowledge sources. Knowledge Servers can provide enterprise- or project-specific context to AI. The importance of context when building AI Coding Assistants or AI Agents. More direction on using MCP to build AI systems that interact with many different tools. From Symptom to Source: AI-Driven Root Cause Analysis in Minutes How AI can support Root Cause Analysis. AI can analyze information from multiple sources to help identify incident causes. Potential to reduce troubleshooting time in system operations. AI can participate in monitoring and operations, not just development. Agent Frameworks and Agent Harness Technologies and frameworks supporting AI Agent development:
Strands. LangGraph. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The role of Agent Frameworks in:
Workflow orchestration. State management. Tool connections. Organizing AI Agent reasoning and execution. Building AI Agents depends not only on Large Language Models but also on proper architecture and orchestration systems.
Data Foundation and Cloud Modernization The role of Data Foundation when deploying AI systems. Data must be well organized, managed and standardized to support AI applications. How Cloud helps enterprises modernize workloads and build scalable architectures. Perspectives on combining Cloud, Data and AI in digital transformation. AWS Local Zones and real-world use cases The role of AWS Local Zones for low-latency workloads.
Typical application groups include:
Banking – Finance. Fintech. Realtime gaming. AI inference. Applications that process data close to users. Perspectives on choosing the right infrastructure based on application latency requirements.
Networking and practical discussions Exchanging ideas on taking AI Agents from prototype to real production environments. Discussing AI Coding, Cloud and cost optimization topics. Further exchanges on challenges of integrating AI into current workflows. Connecting with the AWS Builders community, developers and tech experts in HCMC. What I Learned Agentic AI Clearer understanding of the difference between regular AI chatbots and Agentic AI. AI Agents can use tools, access knowledge and execute multi-step workflows. Agentic AI can participate in many stages of software development and operations. Building AI Agents requires clearly defined scope, tools, data and control mechanisms. AI Agent Architecture Understood that a real-world AI Agent system consists of much more than an LLM:
Large Language Model. Agent Framework. Tools. External APIs. Knowledge Sources. Context Management. Memory. Security. Monitoring. Human validation. Gained additional knowledge of frameworks and platforms such as:
LangGraph. Strands. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. MCP Server. AI in the Software Development Lifecycle AI can be applied across the SDLC:
Planning. Development. Coding. Testing. Security. Delivery. Deployment. Monitoring. Troubleshooting. The shift from traditional Software Development Lifecycle to AI-Native / AI-Driven Development Lifecycle.
AI Coding and MCP The role of Model Context Protocol (MCP) in connecting AI with tools and data sources. MCP can help AI Coding Assistants access project context and external systems. Context and knowledge quality greatly affect AI assistance capabilities. More direction for researching MCP for future AI Agent projects. AI Security How AI can support Application Security. Security should be considered from the design stage. AI can help detect security issues during development and deployment. When building AI Agents, access rights, data and security must all be addressed. AI in system operations The potential of AI in Root Cause Analysis. AI can analyze logs, metrics and system information to support troubleshooting. AI can be used in monitoring and operations, not limited to coding. Data and Cloud Infrastructure The role of Data Foundation for AI systems. Good AI needs quality data and suitable infrastructure architecture. The role of Cloud in providing scalability and flexibility. Perspectives on low-latency workloads and using AWS Local Zones. Applying to Work Research applying AI Agents to current projects instead of only using conventional Q&A models.
Consider Agent Frameworks such as LangGraph or Strands to organize Agent workflows.
Research Amazon Bedrock AgentCore when building AI Agents on AWS.
Explore using MCP Servers to connect AI Agents with:
Tools. APIs. Databases. Knowledge Bases. External systems. Design AI workflows with clear scope and boundary.
Build human validation mechanisms for critical tasks.
Pay attention to security and access rights when Agents can use tools.
Explore bringing AI into more development lifecycle stages:
Coding. Testing. Security. Deployment. Monitoring. Apply an AI-Native Development mindset when building new projects.
Focus on Data Foundation when developing AI-powered applications.
Consider observability and troubleshooting from system design stages.
Continue researching AWS services that support deploying, scaling and operating AI workloads.
Event Experience Attending AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026: HCMC Watch Party at AWS Office HCM was a rewarding experience, helping me catch up on many Cloud and AI trends, especially Agentic AI, AI-Native Software Development and AI-driven Development Lifecycle.
Following in-depth content Followed the Opening Keynote and technical sessions of AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026. Sessions went beyond AI Coding into Agentic AI, security, software development lifecycle and operations. I gained perspectives on how deeply AI is being integrated into system development and operations. Learning more about Agentic AI Agentic AI was one of the event highlights. Learned how AI Agents can use tools and execute complex workflows instead of just generating content. Gained perspectives on the components needed to take AI Agents from prototype to production. This helps orient my future research and Agentic AI projects. Approaching Agent Frameworks and MCP Content on Strands, LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and MCP Server clarified modern AI Agent architecture. The model is only one part of the system; Agents also need tool integration, context, knowledge and orchestration. MCP is a technology worth watching for connecting AI Agents with external systems. Perspectives on AI in the SDLC AI can support much more than code generation. AI is being integrated into security, deployment, monitoring and troubleshooting. AI is becoming a component across the entire Software Development Lifecycle. Connecting and exchanging ideas Networking breaks enabled exchanges with the AWS Builders community in HCMC. Opportunities to discuss AI Agents, Cloud, AI Coding and real-world AI deployment issues. Direct exchanges provided perspectives beyond the technical sessions. Lessons learned An AI Agent is not just an LLM — it combines model, tools, knowledge, workflow and infrastructure. Agentic AI can automate many workflows but needs clear scope and control mechanisms. Agent Frameworks play a key role in organizing and orchestrating AI Agent activity. MCP and Knowledge Integration are components worth watching when building Agents that work with real systems. AI is gradually becoming part of the entire Software Development Lifecycle, not limited to coding. Security and observability must be considered alongside AI automation capabilities. Data Foundation and Cloud Infrastructure are critical foundations when deploying AI at scale. Bringing AI into production requires balancing: Automation capability. Accuracy. Security. Cost. Reliability. Controllability. Some event photos Group photo at the event (3rd person from the photographer in that row).
Group photo at the event (person sitting at the far right end of the front row).
Overall, AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026: HCMC Watch Party not only updated me on Cloud and AI trends but also deepened my understanding of Agentic AI and AI-Native Software Development. Through sharing sessions and networking, I gained knowledge of AI Agent architecture, Agent Frameworks, MCP Server, AI Security, Data Foundation and AI-driven operations. This also helps me better identify technologies to keep researching and apply to future projects.

content:

export TINA_TAG=ws-v1 image() { local name="$1" digest digest="$(aws ecr describe-images --region "$AWS_REGION" --repository-name "tina-staging/$name" --image-ids "imageTag=$TINA_TAG" --query 'imageDetails[0].imageDigest' --output text)" || return 1 [[ "$digest" =~ ^sha256:[a-f0-9]{64}$ ]] || { echo "Digest not found for $name:$TINA_TAG" >&2; return 1; } printf '%s.dkr.ecr.%s.amazonaws.com/tina-staging/%s@%s' "$TINA_ACCOUNT" "$AWS_REGION" "$name" "$digest" } image terminal If you built with a different tag, update TINA_TAG to match. title: Blog 3
content:
Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic – When a Voice Agent Can Do More Than Talk An AI voice assistant is often described as a three-stage pipeline: convert speech to text (Speech-to-Text), send the text to an LLM, and convert the answer back to audio (Text-to-Speech).
This design is familiar and straightforward. However, chaining different components can increase latency in real-time conversations. It also introduces challenges when a user interrupts a response, changes the question, or asks the assistant to carry out an action.
On October 5, 2026, AWS announced Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, a new speech-to-speech model available through Amazon Bedrock, designed for natural real-time conversations and task execution through connected tools.
The interesting aspect is not only voice generation and understanding but also how the model can work with AWS services to create a complete voice agent.
1. What Makes Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic Different? Instead of requiring a separate STT → LLM → TTS pipeline, Nova 2.5 Sonic can take audio input and generate audio output within the same model.
AWS has also improved reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling capabilities compared with Nova 2 Sonic.
Several features stand out:
Real-time speech-to-speech: Two-way voice interactions with low latency. Barge-in: Users can interrupt the agent while it is speaking. Tool calling: The model can request that the application call an API to retrieve information or perform an action. Asynchronous tool calling: The conversation does not always have to stop completely while external tools are running. Cross-modal interaction: Voice and text can be combined in the same session. Tool calling and barge-in are particularly important for voice agents used in real applications.
2. Combining Nova Sonic with AWS Services One possible architecture combines Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime provides a runtime for agents and can support bidirectional WebSocket communication for transmitting and receiving audio. This allows developers to use a managed agent runtime rather than building the entire session infrastructure themselves.
Within the runtime, Strands BidiAgent can manage the conversation session, communicate with Nova Sonic, and handle tool requests.
Amazon Bedrock Amazon Bedrock provides the Nova 2.5 Sonic model, which interprets speech, maintains conversation context, and generates responses.
AgentCore Gateway and AWS Lambda When the agent needs external data, AgentCore Gateway can provide access to MCP-based tools. Behind the gateway, AWS Lambda handles business logic while Amazon DynamoDB stores application data.
The model therefore does not need unrestricted direct access to the database. Business APIs can enforce authorization, validation, and other safeguards.
Supporting Services Amazon S3: Optional audio archive for recorded sessions. Amazon CloudWatch: Logs, traces, and metrics for observability. Amazon Cognito: User sign-in / JWT / temporary credentials for identity and access. Figure 2. AgentCore Runtime architecture for bidirectional voice interactions using Amazon Nova Sonic. Source: AWS Documentation.
3. The Interesting Part: Talking and Completing Tasks Consider a customer-service voice agent.
A customer asks:
“Can you check my latest order?”
The agent invokes a tool to check order status. While the system is retrieving that information, the customer adds:
“Actually, can I change the delivery address?”
A well-designed agent must preserve context, understand the new request, and identify the necessary actions.
If an address change is possible, it can request the corresponding API. However, any actual update must follow access controls, business rules, and appropriate confirmation steps.
This separates an AI system that merely speaks from a voice agent that can interact with external systems.
Another example is when an agent is explaining a delivery policy and the user interrupts:
“Just tell me when it arrives.”
Barge-in support helps the application respond to this interruption rather than forcing the user to listen to the entire previous answer.
Key Capabilities of a Production Voice Agent A production-ready AI Agent requires more than a Large Language Model. Important components include:
LLM: Processes requests and generates responses. Runtime: Provides an environment in which the Agent can execute. Tools and APIs: Allow the Agent to interact with external systems. Memory and Context: Help retain relevant information across interactions. Security and Guardrails: Restrict unsafe operations and protect sensitive resources. Monitoring and Cost Management: Help track usage, performance, and operating expenses. 4. Should Nova 2.5 Sonic Be Used for Every Audio Application? Not necessarily.
Nova 2.5 Sonic is more suited to live voice interaction, such as customer support, appointment scheduling, and spoken information retrieval.
For a workflow that simply converts a recorded audio file into text for storage or later analysis, Amazon Transcribe remains a reasonable option.
AWS lists seven supported languages for Nova 2.5 Sonic, and Vietnamese was not on the officially supported list at the time of this post. This is an important limitation for applications serving Vietnamese-speaking users.
The overall cost is not limited to model usage. AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and other infrastructure components may add operating costs.
5. Conclusion The important shift illustrated by Nova 2.5 Sonic is the move from voice assistants to voice agents.
Rather than only listening and responding, the system can maintain a conversation, retrieve information, and invoke authorized tools to carry out tasks.
Combining Nova Sonic with AgentCore and other AWS services offers developers a practical approach to building real-time conversational applications without managing every part of the agent infrastructure on their own.
This direction is worth exploring as AI applications evolve from answering questions to helping users complete real work.
References AWS – Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic Announcement Amazon Bedrock – Nova 2.5 Sonic Model Card AWS Machine Learning Blog – Build a Voice Travel Concierge Bài viết đã đăng trên AWS Study Group: https://www.facebook.com/groups/awsstudygroupfcj/permalink/2318573642240928/?rdid=KuaalDDzF6dEIiTz#

title: Blogs Posted
content:
During my internship at AWS First Cloud AI Journey, I spent time researching articles from the AWS Blog, combining hands-on lab experience and daily learning to write technical blog posts. Each blog post focuses on a specific topic, helping me consolidate knowledge, share experiences, and introduce solutions and best practices on AWS. My goal is to contribute practical, accessible content to the AWS Study Group community that can be applied directly to real-world work.
The following blog posts were shared on AWS Study Group:
Blog 1 - Amazon Transcribe vs OpenAI Whisper: Which Speech-to-Text Solution Fits Vietnamese? Amazon Transcribe and OpenAI Whisper approach the same speech-to-text problem from two different directions: a fully managed AWS service and an open-source model that teams can self-host. The post compares Vietnamese recognition quality, deployment models, operating costs, and the trade-offs between convenience and control. It also walks through practical AWS architectures, from batch transcription to near-real-time streaming, and explains how to evaluate results objectively with Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER). Rather than assuming one option is better, the article shows how to benchmark both solutions on the same Vietnamese dataset and choose based on accuracy, budget, and operational requirements.
Blog 2 - From Meeting Transcripts to Notion Tasks with DynamoDB Streams, Lambda and Bedrock The post describes an event-driven pipeline that starts automatically when a meeting transcript is marked as completed in DynamoDB. DynamoDB Streams triggers AWS Lambda, which reads the transcript from Amazon S3, calls Amazon Bedrock to extract action items, and stores the proposed tasks for human review before creating them in Notion. The article explains each step in detail, including the Lambda handler, prompt design, idempotency checks, human confirmation, and cost considerations. It also discusses how the same pattern can be extended to email, support tickets, call-center transcripts, and other task management tools, making it a reusable blueprint for serverless automation.
Blog 3 - Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic: From Voice Assistants to Task-Performing Voice Agents The post examines Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic, a speech-to-speech model on Amazon Bedrock that aims to replace the traditional STT → LLM → TTS pipeline with a single real-time model. It covers low-latency voice interaction, barge-in, tool calling, asynchronous tool use, and cross-modal sessions, then shows how Nova Sonic can be combined with AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB to build a complete voice agent. The article also discusses practical use cases, current language limitations, cost and operational considerations, and when a simpler transcription service such as Amazon Transcribe is still the better choice.

title: Single CloudFormation deployment
content:
Fast deployment overview (5 commands in CloudShell) Download tina-full.yml The tina-full.yml template provisions the entire TINA infrastructure in a single stack: a 2-AZ VPC, NAT Gateway, S3, CloudFront + WAF, an internal ALB, RDS PostgreSQL, ElastiCache Valkey, ECS Fargate (ARM64), Terminal, Bot, Runtime, VieGem ASR, Agent API, Agent Reach, MCP, Flows, and workspace storage.
The entire deployment is split into 5 short sequential commands in AWS CloudShell (us-east-1)—wait for each command to finish before running the next, with no EC2 builder or local Docker build required:
Command 1: Set up environment variables, the ECS service-linked role, and the crane tool. Command 2: Copy all 15 prebuilt linux/arm64 images (12 core images including VieGem + 3 Voice images livekit, livekit-agent, vieneu) from GHCR into your ECR. Command 3: Look up Managed Prefix Lists (CloudFront, S3) and upload tina-full.yml to a temporary S3 bucket. Command 4: Create the tina-workshop-full stack, wait for completion, and retrieve WebsiteUrl. Command 5: Attach your own Google OAuth credentials to enable web sign-in. Note: Run in the us-east-1 Region and avoid deploying on top of an account that already has tina-staging-* stacks. If you are using an AWS Free Plan account, check your RDS quota first (Free Plan limits the number of RDS instances—if another RDS instance already exists, you may hit ServiceLimitExceeded). The VieGem model is licensed for non-commercial use under CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 and the Gemma terms (model card ).
Command 1 — Prepare CloudShell, ECS role, and ECR login Open AWS CloudShell in the us-east-1 Region, paste the following command, and press Enter:
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 export AWS_PAGER='' export STACK_NAME=tina-workshop-full export AWS_ACCOUNT="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)" export ECR_REG="${AWS_ACCOUNT}.dkr.ecr.${AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com" # Create the ECS service-linked role (only needed on accounts that have never run ECS) aws iam get-role --role-name AWSServiceRoleForECS >/dev/null 2>&1 \ || aws iam create-service-linked-role --aws-service-name ecs.amazonaws.com # Download crane into /tmp to copy images directly from CloudShell (no Docker needed) if [ ! -x /tmp/crane ]; then curl -sSL "https://github.com/google/go-containerregistry/releases/latest/download/go-containerregistry_Linux_x86_64.tar.gz" \ | tar -xz -C /tmp crane fi # Authenticate crane against your account's ECR registry aws ecr get-login-password --region "$AWS_REGION" \ | /tmp/crane auth login "$ECR_REG" -u AWS --password-stdin echo "OK: Account=$AWS_ACCOUNT | ECR=$ECR_REG" Explanation: This command fetches your AWS account ID (AWS_ACCOUNT), ensures AWSServiceRoleForECS exists, downloads the crane binary (~8 MB), and logs into ECR. Once you see OK: Account=..., Command 1 is complete.
Command 2 — Copy all 15 ARM64 images (including VieGem & Voice) from GHCR to ECR Paste the command below to create 15 tina-staging/* repositories in ECR and copy all 15 linux/arm64 images from ghcr.io/poor-frog/tina-*:workshop-arm64 into your ECR (takes about 2–3 minutes):
GHCR_PREFIX="ghcr.io/poor-frog" GHCR_TAG="workshop-arm64" SERVICES=(terminal gateway meeting-api admin-api runtime bot agent-api agent-reach agent-worker mcp flows viegem livekit livekit-agent vieneu) : > /tmp/tina-digests.env for name in "${SERVICES[@]}"; do aws ecr describe-repositories --region "$AWS_REGION" --repository-names "tina-staging/$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 \ || aws ecr create-repository --region "$AWS_REGION" --repository-name "tina-staging/$name" \ --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE --encryption-configuration encryptionType=AES256 >/dev/null echo ">>> Copying $name..." /tmp/crane copy "${GHCR_PREFIX}/tina-${name}:${GHCR_TAG}" "${ECR_REG}/tina-staging/${name}:${GHCR_TAG}" DIGEST="$(aws ecr describe-images --region "$AWS_REGION" --repository-name "tina-staging/$name" \ --image-ids "imageTag=${GHCR_TAG}" --query 'imageDetails[0].imageDigest' --output text)" VAR_NAME="$(echo "$name" | tr '[:lower:]-' '[:upper:]_')_DIGEST" echo "export ${VAR_NAME}=${DIGEST}" >> /tmp/tina-digests.env done source /tmp/tina-digests.env echo "=== Saved all 15 digests to /tmp/tina-digests.env ===" cat /tmp/tina-digests.env Explanation: Instead of launching an ARM64 EC2 instance and building Docker images for 1–2 hours, crane copy transfers all 15 images (12 core images including VieGem + 3 Voice images livekit, livekit-agent, vieneu) directly from GHCR to ECR and records all 15 sha256:... digests in /tmp/tina-digests.env. Wait until all 15 export ..._DIGEST=sha256:... lines are printed before moving to Command 3.
▶ Advanced option: build all 12 images from source on an ARM64 EC2 instance (without GHCR) If you want to build from commit 8a2b79e884bc0833f9075d4e795b20d347cef9c2 yourself, follow the ARM64 EC2 setup and inline /root/tina-ecr-build.sh script in 5.4.1 S3, ECR, and ARM64 image builds and run it with the --full flag.
Command 3 — Look up Prefix Lists & upload tina-full.yml to temporary S3 Download tina-full.yml using the button at the top of this page, click Actions → Upload file in CloudShell to upload it to your home directory ~/ (i.e. ~/tina-full.yml), then run:
CF_PL="$(aws ec2 describe-managed-prefix-lists --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --filters Name=prefix-list-name,Values=com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing \ --query 'PrefixLists[0].PrefixListId' --output text)" S3_PL="$(aws ec2 describe-managed-prefix-lists --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --filters Name=prefix-list-name,Values=com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3 \ --query 'PrefixLists[0].PrefixListId' --output text)" TPL_BUCKET="tina-cfn-tpl-${AWS_ACCOUNT}-${AWS_REGION}" aws s3 mb "s3://${TPL_BUCKET}" --region "$AWS_REGION" 2>/dev/null || true aws s3 cp ~/tina-full.yml "s3://${TPL_BUCKET}/tina-full.yml" --region "$AWS_REGION" echo "OK: CF_PL=$CF_PL | S3_PL=$S3_PL | TPL=https://${TPL_BUCKET}.s3.${AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com/tina-full.yml" Explanation:
CF_PL and S3_PL are the two AWS Managed Prefix List IDs in us-east-1, used to lock down Security Groups so only CloudFront and S3 traffic is allowed. Because tina-full.yml (~151 KB) exceeds CloudFormation’s 51 KB inline template limit, it must be uploaded to a temporary S3 bucket so CloudFormation can read it via --template-url. Command 4 — Create stack tina-workshop-full and get WebsiteUrl Paste the command below to create the entire stack and wait for AWS to finish provisioning (RDS + Valkey + CloudFront + ECS takes about 12–18 minutes):
source /tmp/tina-digests.env aws cloudformation create-stack --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name "$STACK_NAME" \ --template-url "https://${TPL_BUCKET}.s3.${AWS_REGION}.amazonaws.com/tina-full.yml" \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM \ --parameters \ ParameterKey=CloudFrontOriginPrefixListId,ParameterValue="$CF_PL" \ ParameterKey=S3PrefixListId,ParameterValue="$S3_PL" \ ParameterKey=WorkspaceOwnerIds,ParameterValue="" \ ParameterKey=GoogleSecretArn,ParameterValue="" \ ParameterKey=EnableVoice,ParameterValue="false" \ ParameterKey=VoicePilotRoom,ParameterValue="" \ ParameterKey=BotDigest,ParameterValue="$BOT_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=RuntimeDigest,ParameterValue="$RUNTIME_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=AdminDigest,ParameterValue="$ADMIN_API_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=MeetingDigest,ParameterValue="$MEETING_API_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=GatewayDigest,ParameterValue="$GATEWAY_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=TerminalDigest,ParameterValue="$TERMINAL_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=AgentApiDigest,ParameterValue="$AGENT_API_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=AgentWorkerDigest,ParameterValue="$AGENT_WORKER_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=AgentReachDigest,ParameterValue="$AGENT_REACH_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=McpDigest,ParameterValue="$MCP_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=FlowsDigest,ParameterValue="$FLOWS_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=VieGemDigest,ParameterValue="$VIEGEM_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=VieNeuDigest,ParameterValue="$VIENEU_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=LiveKitDigest,ParameterValue="$LIVEKIT_DIGEST" \ ParameterKey=LiveKitAgentDigest,ParameterValue="$LIVEKIT_AGENT_DIGEST" echo "Waiting for CloudFormation stack creation (~12-18 minutes)..." aws cloudformation wait stack-create-complete --region "$AWS_REGION" --stack-name "$STACK_NAME" WEBSITE_URL="$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name "$STACK_NAME" \ --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='WebsiteUrl'].OutputValue" --output text)" echo "WebsiteUrl: $WEBSITE_URL" curl -sS "${WEBSITE_URL}/edge-health" && echo "" Explanation:
GoogleSecretArn is left empty on initial creation because you need the CloudFront-generated WebsiteUrl before registering the Redirect URI in Google. When finished, curl .../edge-health prints TINA_EDGE_READY, and opening WebsiteUrl in your browser shows the TINA landing page. Single-file CloudFormation stack with account ID and ARNs redacted in the parameter list. Command 5 — Attach your own Google OAuth for web sign-in Open the Google Cloud Console → Google Auth Platform → Clients → Create client → Web application. Add an Authorized redirect URI matching WebsiteUrl from Command 4: https://<your-cloudfront-domain>/api/auth/callback/google Save it to obtain your Client ID and Client secret (if the app is in Testing mode, add your Gmail address under Test users). Configuring the Google OAuth Web application client and Authorized redirect URI in Google Cloud Console. Return to CloudShell, replace PASTE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and PASTE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, and run the final command: umask 077 GOOGLE_JSON="$(mktemp)" cat > "$GOOGLE_JSON" <<'EOF' {"client_id":"PASTE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID","client_secret":"PASTE_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET"} EOF GOOGLE_SECRET_ARN="$(aws secretsmanager create-secret --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --name "${STACK_NAME}-google-oauth" --secret-string "file://$GOOGLE_JSON" \ --query ARN --output text)" rm -f -- "$GOOGLE_JSON" aws cloudformation update-stack --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name "$STACK_NAME" \ --use-previous-template \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM \ --parameters \ ParameterKey=CloudFrontOriginPrefixListId,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=S3PrefixListId,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=WorkspaceOwnerIds,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=GoogleSecretArn,ParameterValue="$GOOGLE_SECRET_ARN" \ ParameterKey=EnableVoice,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=VoicePilotRoom,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=BotDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=RuntimeDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=AdminDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=MeetingDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=GatewayDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=TerminalDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=AgentApiDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=AgentWorkerDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=AgentReachDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=McpDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=FlowsDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=VieGemDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=VieNeuDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=LiveKitDigest,UsePreviousValue=true \ ParameterKey=LiveKitAgentDigest,UsePreviousValue=true aws cloudformation wait stack-update-complete --region "$AWS_REGION" --stack-name "$STACK_NAME" echo "DONE! Open $WEBSITE_URL to sign in with Google." Explanation: This command stores your Google OAuth credentials in Secrets Manager (and immediately removes the temporary file from CloudShell), then updates the Terminal container to receive GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET. Wait ~1–2 minutes for Terminal to restart, then sign in with Google to use the web app, bot, and VieGem.
Voice and cleanup when finished Voice (optional): All 3 linux/arm64 images for the Voice stack (livekit, livekit-agent, vieneu) were already copied into ECR by Command 2 and passed into the stack in Command 4. To enable Voice, simply run update-stack with EnableVoice=true and your VoicePilotRoom (keeping UsePreviousValue=true for all other parameters). Cleanup: Run aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name tina-workshop-full --region us-east-1, then review and remove retained resources (DeletionPolicy: Retain: S3 buckets, KMS key, RDS snapshot) following 5.6 Cleanup and evidence .

title: Validate the application
content:
1. Check the website and sign-in If you used the single-stack template , get WebsiteUrl from Outputs to verify the landing page. The combined stack does not configure sign-in until you attach Google OAuth, so the post-sign-in checks on this page apply primarily to the multi-stack path (or after completing Command 5 of the single-stack path).
Retrieve the CloudFront URL created in your account:
stackout tina-ws-edge StageUrl Open the URL in your browser. Verify that the TINA page loads, then sign in with the Google test user you registered. Capture a screenshot of the sign-in page from your own environment:
TINA sign-in page on your CloudFront URL; redact email addresses and domains if sharing. If sign-in fails, verify that the Google OAuth client belongs to the right project, the callback URI matches StageUrl exactly, the user is listed under Test users, the secret JSON has the exact two keys, and Terminal is Running. Inspect the Terminal logs without exposing secret values.
2. Run a test meeting Create a test meeting with the consent of all participants. In TINA, create a meeting through the UI, enter the test meeting URL, and start it. Watch the bot join, confirm the bot task appears in ECS, and verify the meeting status updates. The meeting provider, lobby admission, or participant permissions can affect whether the bot can enter the room; if it fails to join, record the error and check the bot logs, runtime logs, Fargate quotas, NAT gateway, and meeting room policy.
Consented test meeting and bot status; use dummy data and redact participant details. If you enabled VieGem properly and audio streaming succeeds, speak a non-sensitive test phrase, wait for the transcript to appear, and verify its accuracy. If ASR is not enabled or no transcript appears, record Not passed / Not tested—do not fabricate screenshots.
Transcript of a non-sensitive test phrase once ASR is working. End the meeting and confirm that the bot task stops. If recording is enabled, check the test meeting’s object metadata in your own bucket; do not include private audio or transcripts in any report.
3. Record actual results Check Expected result Observation Web CloudFront URL renders Terminal Pass/Fail and timestamp Sign-in Google test user signs in to TINA Pass/Fail, without recording secrets ECS Runtime, core, and Terminal are stable; target is healthy desired/running counts, events Meeting Bot joins the test room and stops after the meeting Actual result Transcription Transcript appears when ASR is configured Pass/Fail or not configured A CREATE_COMPLETE stack only confirms that the infrastructure was provisioned—it does not replace this application validation. title: Event 4
content:
Event Takeaways: “AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day” Event Objectives Learn how engineering teams approach software development at scale, including the practical challenges of building Software Factories. Explore the skills students need to bridge academic learning and real-world Cloud and software engineering work. Understand the ideas presented in the AWS Lambda Web Functions session, particularly HTTP handling, request concurrency, performance and cost considerations. Explore how Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) can decouple components and support asynchronous system design. Learn from an AWS internship journey and explore ways to begin and maintain contributions to open-source projects. Connect the technical topics to future Cloud projects and professional development. Speakers The event poster introduced six speakers from industry and the FCAJ community:
Thinh Nguyen – STYL Solutions. Henry Duc Bui – CloudThinker. Hung Tran – NAB. Dao Cu Long – FCAJ. Khang Duong – FCAJ. Tuan Tran – FCAJ. The event was scheduled for 9:00 AM–12:00 PM on Saturday, October 31, 2026, at the 26th floor of Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Ho Chi Minh City.
Key Highlights Lessons Learned from Building Software Factories (9:00–9:25 AM) The session focused on practical lessons from building Software Factories at scale rather than treating software delivery as a series of isolated coding tasks. Its agenda highlighted common implementation pitfalls and the importance of identifying approaches that work in real engineering teams. A useful topic for further study is how standardized workflows, automation and feedback loops support predictable software delivery. The session provides a reason to examine maintainability and developer experience alongside deployment speed. Education (9:30–9:55 AM) This session examined how students can prepare for Cloud and software engineering careers from an educator’s perspective. It addressed the gap between university learning and expectations in the workplace. Technical fundamentals, hands-on projects, communication and independent problem-solving are all relevant areas for students to reflect on. The discussion topic emphasizes that completing tutorials is different from explaining design decisions and working within a team. AWS Lambda Web Functions: Rethinking Serverless Web Architecture (10:00–10:25 AM) The session introduced an approach to Serverless web applications involving native HTTP support and multi-concurrency of up to 128 requests, as described in the event agenda. It raised the question of when a Serverless approach can reduce adapter overhead compared with alternative deployment patterns. Active CPU Billing was included as a topic for analyzing cost efficiency rather than considering only the number of invocations. Performance benchmarking against container-based workloads on Amazon EC2 or Amazon ECS was part of the announced session scope. The key architectural question is how latency, request patterns, scaling behavior and total operating costs affect platform selection. Amazon SQS: Building Asynchronous Systems (10:30–11:00 AM) Amazon SQS was presented as a building block for asynchronous processing and decoupling services. Queues allow work to be buffered rather than requiring every request to be completed immediately by a downstream component. A practical design should account for retries, visibility timeouts, duplicate messages and dead-letter queues where appropriate. An example is a file-processing application: the upload service receives a file, while workers independently process queued tasks. The session topic illustrates how asynchronous design can improve resilience and help systems handle fluctuating workloads. My 3-Month AWS Internship Journey (11:00–11:25 AM) This session shared a three-month internship perspective, including the use of AWS services in a real project. A relevant lesson is to connect technical exercises with clear project objectives and measurable outcomes. Cloud projects involve more than launching resources: security, monitoring, documentation, cost and troubleshooting also matter. The session offered a useful context for reviewing learning progress and preparing for the transition from university projects to professional work. Start & Maintain Consistency with Open Source Contributing (11:30 AM–12:00 PM) The session focused on how to begin contributing to open-source projects and maintain a consistent contribution habit. Contributions can start with documentation, issue reproduction, small bug fixes or tests instead of large feature implementations. Reviewing contribution guidelines and working with Git branches and pull requests are practical skills to develop. Regular, manageable contributions can help build familiarity with collaborative software development and code review. What I Learned Software Engineering and Career Preparation A sustainable software delivery process needs clear conventions, repeatable workflows and feedback, not only faster coding. Engineering skills grow when academic concepts are applied to practical systems and their trade-offs can be explained. Internship projects should be documented with their goals, architecture, technical decisions and results. Serverless Architecture and Cost Awareness Serverless design choices should be evaluated using workload characteristics such as request volume, execution time, concurrency and latency. Performance benchmarks need comparable conditions before conclusions can be drawn about AWS Lambda, EC2 or ECS. Cost analysis should include more than the advertised compute rate: supporting services, operational overhead and idle capacity can influence the final result. The Lambda Web Functions claims in the agenda are useful starting points for further documentation review and hands-on validation. Asynchronous Processing with Amazon SQS A queue separates the rate at which requests arrive from the rate at which workers process them. Producers and consumers can be scaled and deployed independently when the application is designed around a queue. Reliability requires thoughtful handling of retries, idempotency, failed messages and monitoring of queue depth. Asynchronous processing is particularly relevant for workloads such as video conversion, background notifications and audio transcription. Open Source and Continuous Learning Small, consistent contributions are a practical way to gain experience with real codebases. Reading existing code and documentation is an important part of contributing effectively. Technical growth also depends on communication, collaboration and the habit of evaluating lessons from completed work. Applying to Work Review project development workflows for opportunities to automate testing, builds, deployment and documentation. Compare Serverless and EC2/ECS deployment options using realistic request patterns, latency targets and cost assumptions. Explore Amazon SQS for asynchronous tasks that do not need to complete within the user-facing HTTP request. Design background workers with retry handling, visibility timeouts, idempotency and dead-letter queue policies. Apply the event’s Cloud engineering themes to project documentation: explain the architecture, permissions, monitoring and operational trade-offs. Build a sustainable open-source learning routine, beginning with small, reviewable contributions. Event Experience The AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day brought together software engineering, Cloud architecture and professional development topics in one morning. The program combined industry perspectives with sessions relevant to students preparing for Cloud and software development roles.
Connecting Architecture with Real-World Decisions The Software Factories session raised questions about the processes required to develop and maintain software at scale. The AWS Lambda Web Functions topic connected Serverless architecture with performance measurement and cost evaluation. The Amazon SQS topic showed why communication patterns matter when applications grow beyond a single service. Connecting Learning with Professional Practice The Education and internship sessions highlighted the importance of hands-on learning and explaining technical choices. The open-source topic provided a concrete direction for practicing team workflows outside the classroom. Together, these themes encourage a balance between technical depth and steady professional development. Networking and Personal Development The program offered an opportunity to engage with AWS and software engineering topics from different professional perspectives. Its mixture of technical and career-focused sessions offers useful directions for further study, particularly distributed systems and developer workflows. Specific discussion points and personal observations can be added here from event notes before the final report is submitted. Lessons Learned Engineering is more than code: processes and collaboration influence how software is delivered. Evaluate Serverless with evidence: latency, concurrency and cost should be measured for the target workload. Decoupling supports scalability: asynchronous queues help separate components and smooth workload spikes. Operational details matter: retries, monitoring and failure handling are essential in production systems. Internships connect theory and practice: real projects require architectural reasoning and clear communication. Consistency supports growth: regular open-source contributions can strengthen long-term engineering skills. Some Event Photos AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day (third person from the right).
Overall, AWS First Cloud AI Journey Community Day offered an opportunity to connect software delivery practices, Serverless design, asynchronous processing and career preparation. The sessions provide useful directions for further exploration: comparing Cloud architectures with measurable criteria, using queues where asynchronous processing is appropriate, documenting AWS internship projects carefully and developing a consistent approach to open-source learning.

title: Scope and extensions
content:
What is configured This path deploys a complete meetings test environment: Terminal, Google sign-in, core services, Runtime launching ECS bot tasks, storage, and optional VieGem. This flow has been verified end-to-end on an independent AWS account across Google sign-in, meeting bot participation, and VieGem transcription.
Optional Extensions Ready to Deploy Amazon Bedrock (amazon.nova-lite-v1:0): The single-stack template in 5.4A already grants bedrock:InvokeModel permissions for amazon.nova-lite-v1:0 (bedrock-converse) to power notes, summaries, and the Agent. On a fresh account, open Amazon Bedrock → Model catalog in us-east-1 to confirm access to Amazon Nova Lite. Amazon SES (Post-meeting follow-up emails): Requires a custom domain hosted in Route 53 (for DKIM, SPF, and DMARC DNS records), so it is not enabled by default in the base lab. Once you have a domain, deploy deploy/aws/staging-ses.yml from the project’s main branch (provisions SES ConfigurationSet, EmailIdentity, Route 53 DNS records, SMTP credentials in Secrets Manager, and 3 CloudWatch reputation alarms for bounces/complaints): aws cloudformation deploy --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --stack-name tina-ws-ses \ --template-file deploy/aws/staging-ses.yml \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM \ --parameter-overrides \ DomainName=your-domain.example \ HostedZoneId=Z1234567890ABC \ AlertEmail=ops@your-domain.example CloudWatch Dashboard & Operational Alarms: In addition to the 13 built-in Log Groups, main includes deploy/aws/staging-workspace-s3-monitoring.yml (10 Metric Filters, 20 CloudWatch Alarms covering ALB 5xx, ECS memory ≥85%, RDS CPU/storage/connections, and S3 sync, plus a unified CloudWatch Dashboard) and deploy/aws/apply-ecr-lifecycle.sh to expire old ECR images automatically. Workspace/agent workbench & Voice (LiveKit/VieNeu): The multi-stack walkthrough deploys the lightweight meetings tier; to enable the full Workspace, Agent, MCP, Flows, and Voice stack, use the combined template in 5.4A with all 15 workshop-arm64 images. Production operations: Additional SSO providers, custom domains (staging-domain-acm.yml), Multi-AZ/backup, and automated CI/CD (staging-github-ecr.yml) are available as reference templates in deploy/aws on main .
